priorities.description:
SEND THE CONCORDIA ACCESS LETTER. Researched and drafted 2026-08-25 -- the full plan, the named people, the four configuration options, the fee schedule and a ready-to-send draft are at project-docs/concordia-access-plan.md. ADDRESSEE: John Richan, Interim Director and University Archivist (also listed as Digital Archivist), via archives@concordia.ca; five-working-day response target. THE ASK IS FOUR THINGS IN ONE LETTER: (1) P0145/12C01 the 1936 Otoreke mixed-camp evaluation, Box HA2315; (2) 12B02, 12B05 and 12B06, the three Kanawana sub-sub-series with no public page; (3) an object list for 12B (t-shirts, badges, ribbons, pennants, film reels); (4) a REST API key plus the REST API added to endpoint_exceptions -- AtoM's own documented configuration for programmatic access, which leaves the JS challenge in force for ordinary traffic. NEEDS MATT: only he can send it. ADDENDUM 2026-08-25 (p_278): add the AV reproduction request to the same letter. Highest value, in order: P0145-11-0193 'Kamp Kanawana - Interview with Woodsman', 24 Aug 1962; P0145-11-0197 'What is God? / Interview of Kamp Kanawana campers and staff', 1963; P0145-11-0191 'Pathfinder evaluation' (bears on the coeducation open question). AV reproduction is $1.00/minute for scholarly use -- these are cheap.

priorities.description: The Green Triangle has a 36-year hole in the digitized run: issues exist for 1932-1940 and 1976-1982, with NOTHING between. The 1947 volume would document the Lumbermen-Voyageurs origin contemporaneously rather than through the 1988 retrospective, and the 1940s-50s issues would attack the 1947-1958 director gap.
priorities.notes: 2026-08-25: all 38 DIGITIZED issues downloaded, verified, read in full and cached at sources/cache/green-triangle/. The 36-year hole is CONFIRMED REAL, not a search artefact: the run is dense 1932-1940 (36 issues), then only 1976-09 and 1982-11-15. What remains is the undigitized 1941-1975 material at Concordia -- which is now part of the p_282 letter rather than a separate web-research task.

The Feb 1959 issue OCRs cleanly and the whole run is full-text searchable. Canadian Camping Magazine is the national trade journal of the period and would carry Kanawana programme notes, staff moves and conference reports. NOTE the Phase 2 trap: use the full-text endpoint, not advancedsearch.php, which indexes metadata only.

priorities.description: OPERATOR ACTION: request three folders from Trent University Archives (archives@trentu.ca, 705-748-1011 x7413; access explicitly unrestricted). (1) OCA fonds 72-007, Series 1, Box 1, Folder 5 -- a KANAWANA BROCHURE DATED 1940. (2) OCA fonds 78-006, Series F, Box 24, Folder 25 -- a Kanawana brochure c.1970s, filed among 'Y' camps with Pine Crest. (3) 84-019, Box 1, Folder 10 -- 'YMCA - Montreal'. The 1940 brochure is the single highest-value unread document this project has ever located: it sits OUTSIDE the YMCA's own archive, so it is independent corroboration, and it covers a decade the wiki is thin on. A brochure typically carries fees, session dates, programme, section names and staff.

priorities.description: HEAR THE 1962 AND 1963 CAMPER RECORDINGS. P0145-11-0193 'Kamp Kanawana - Interview with Woodsman' (24 August 1962) and P0145-11-0197 'What is God? / Interview of Kamp Kanawana campers and staff' (1963) are dated oral recordings of campers and staff from a decade this wiki documents almost entirely through annual reports and brochures. They are the closest thing to oral history that exists for the period, and unlike the operator-interview instrument planned under CLAUDE.md's pending priority, they are CONTEMPORANEOUS rather than recalled. Reproduction is $1.00/minute for scholarly use. Also check whether RMA has already posted them to its YouTube channel, as it did with P0145-09-0066 'Canoe Trips' in February 2026. Folded into the p_282 letter; listed separately because its value is independent of the rest.

priorities.description: Locate The Lookout issues 1 and 2, and any 1994 centennial issues. Only Vol.1 No.3 (autumn 1993) is digitized, and it alone yielded Itche Kerr's first-person account of writing the camp song, the only source for Tom Potts as 1972 director, the 1993 L&V result, and the Maureen McBride memorial. The newsletter gives a contact address and phone and names dozens of alumni contributors. A centennial issue would be the richest single document available.

Issues 1, 2 and any centennial issue must be requested from Concordia; ADDED TO THE p_282 LETTER. Byproduct: the parent collection ymca-montreal-fonds holds 1,037 items to our 634; the 403 difference is digitized PHOTOGRAPHS (sampled, all mediatype image, no text layer), not unread documents. Three are Kanawana (2001 team-building). See f_2293.

priorities.description: The 1969 camper drowning: find the name and date. Recorded in the Kanawana annual report as "the tragic drowing of one of our campers this Summer" with no further detail. Quebec coroner records, the Montreal Star and Gazette for summer 1969, and Concordia's physical Kanawana holdings are the routes. Handle with care -- a child's death, family very possibly living. Establish the facts; decide publication separately with the operator.
priorities.notes: 2026-08-25: NOT ESTABLISHED. The 1969 annual report line is the only attestation; a full-text sweep of all 634 corpus documents for 'drow*' found every OTHER drowning in the association's record but nothing further on 1969, and the open web has nothing. Remaining routes are the Gazette/Star for summer 1969, Quebec coroner records, and Concordia's physical holdings. Recommend the operator decide whether to pursue a named identification at all before more effort is spent -- see f_2294.

priorities.description: For the ORAL HISTORY INSTRUMENT (p_045 Chopsy). The documentary record on Chopsy is now EXHAUSTED: zero hits across all 634 digitized text items. But two findings reframe the question. (1) "The Cave" in the legend is a real camp building doing exactly what the story says -- the 1987 report has it as the hike-and-trip equipment store. (2) The Haunted House is documented 1928-1940 with its own ghost legend and its own rule (spirits appear only when the wind is from the east and the moon and stars invisible), and stops just before Chopsy's stated 1945 origin. ASK: is Chopsy a successor to, or renaming of, the Haunted House ghost? Also ask about "the deserted village" the 1933 newsletter has campers passing en route.
Collect oral history on 'Chopsy' legend from Matt Aronson — full narrative, origin period, telling context, location ties, jump-scare elements
priorities.blocking_reason: Requires oral history input from domain expert (src_oral_aronson). No online sources exist for this story.

priorities.description: Confirm or refute the O. N. H. Owens identification behind the Order of Owens. He is documented in Montreal YMCA camping service 1929-1964 -- Chairman of the Kanawana Committee in 1937-38 (named on the camp's own letterhead beside Director W. J. G. Macdiarmid), Chairman of Camp Perrot's Board of Management through the 1940s-50s. A Library and Archives Canada First World War file exists for "OWENS, OWEN NORREYS HARRINGTON" -- initials match, "Norrey" is the natural short form of Norreys -- but the LAC record returns Cloudflare 403 to automated fetch and needs a human or an authenticated route. Also still unknown: what April 13, 1976 commemorates.
priorities.notes: 2026-08-25: THE INTERNAL IDENTIFICATION IS MADE. Norrey Owens = O. N. H. Owens, established by the Quebec Camping Association presidency which both forms of the name hold (QCA President June 1954; O.N.H. Owens on the January 1976 membership roll; 'Norrey Owens' listed among QCA past presidents March 1977). Service span extended 1929-1977. STILL OPEN and now the whole of the task: (a) the LAC First World War file for 'OWENS, OWEN NORREYS HARRINGTON' -- Cloudflare 403 to automated fetch, needs a human or authenticated route; (b) birth and death dates; (c) what 13 April 1976 commemorates -- the corpus sweep found nothing, and the article already establishes it is NOT a death date since Owens presented the award in person that August.

priorities.description: Commission de toponymie du Quebec: settle the lake name changes. The official toponymic record should give (a) the date and rationale of Lac Saint-Louis -> Lac Kanawana, (b) the same for Lac Desjardins -> Lac Wilson, and (c) whether 'Kanawana' has a documented Indigenous-language etymology or is an invented coinage. Surfaced by the p_263 RALPH loop as the highest-value UNFETCHED geographic source in the project. Made sharper by the MIR reconciliation article, which shows genuine Indigenous names and invented pseudo-Indigenous names are equally common in North American camping -- so the question is real, not rhetorical. Also try the Quebec lake registry / RSVL for real bathymetry, since the only area and shoreline figures currently held are from a commercial chart aggregator that disclaims them.

priorities.description: Unmined seams the annual-report sweep identified but did not attempt: (a) the Kanawana balance-sheet property valuations, present in every report from 1925 (e.g. $17,876.39 in 1925, $55,750.30 in 1949, $70,567.80 in 1951) -- a clean book-value series across eighty years, but the columnar OCR is heavily damaged and each figure needs verification against the page image; (b) the World/Foreign Service contribution tables, which carry a Kanawana line every year 1923-1964 from the campers' Sunday collections; (c) the French editions of the 1982-2009 reports, which were spot-checked as translations but not read independently.

Two cataloguing defects to work around and, if possible, report to Concordia/IA: (1) "sgw-ymca-annual-report-1990-1991" and "-1991-1992" hold 1890-91 and 1891-92 content -- misdated by a century, and the 1890-91 one announces W. H. Ball's hiring; (2) the Kanawana orienteering map catalogued as 1974 is internally c.1978-1982 (it shows Katimavik, the sauna and the Grand Portage). Anyone searching that collection by date will miss or misdate these.

priorities.description: The official Kanawana Flickr account (flickr.com/photos/kanawana/) has approximately 26 uncatalogued albums (thousands of photos, roughly 2009-2013 era) beyond the single 'Plaque' album already mined extensively for director/staff facts. This is the single largest untapped source surfaced by the Phase 2 broad-sweep campaign. Given the volume, needs an operator decision on scope before diving in: mine all albums systematically, sample a subset, or prioritize by album title/date first.

Two physical artifacts worth photographing or tracing at camp. (1) The dining hall's "striking, large fireplace mural" of the Lumbermen/Voyageur motif, described in the 1950 annual report and absent from every modern description of the room -- did it survive? (2) "The ancient plaques that haunt the dining hall", per the 1993 alumni newsletter.

Who was M. E. Williams, and what was the full span of the M. E. Williams cups? A previously unknown Kanawana competition with a documented winners roll 1917-1922, inter-branch (North Branch / Central / Westmount) rather than the L&V two-team format. Unknown: who Williams was, when the cups were first given, when they lapsed, and whether they are an ancestor of the L&V Games or an unrelated tradition. ALSO: obtain a PAGE IMAGE of the 1923 Gas Bag Extra to confirm the ditto marks in the winners table -- the OCR renders them as garbage characters, so the repeat years are currently an inference. The annual reports for 1918-1923 are the obvious first place to look for Williams and for the cups' origin.

Pursue Quebec vital-records/genealogy sources (Drouin collection, Ancestry Quebec) to determine whether Rob Braide (broadcaster, b. 1953, chaired the Kanawana Capital Campaign) is related to the separate Braide family of David Ian William Braide (1928-2018) -> Robbie David Braide -> Ian/Vicki Braide (2000s campers/CITs) -- both families have independent Montreal-area YMCA ties but no source found links them directly.

Reclassify src_ebay_valcartier_ymca_postcard. It is filed as Kanawana-relevant material culture, but Camp Valcartier is a First World War ARMY training camp near Quebec City with a YMCA wartime presence -- about 250 km from Saint-Sauveur, with no documented Montreal YMCA or boys'-camping connection. It is weak on-topic evidence even if the listing were readable, and it is not: eBay returns HTTP 403 anti-bot refusals, so the listing body has never been seen. Library and Archives Canada and the Canadian War Museum hold the same subject matter in permanent citable form.

priorities.description: THE BIG SEAM -- NUMBERS CORRECTED 2026-08-25. The Concordia-digitized YMCA of Montreal fonds on Internet Archive holds 1,037 items. Measured this session: 634 are text and are ALREADY HELD LOCALLY and have been swept repeatedly; the other 403 are digitized PHOTOGRAPHS with no text layer (12-item random sample, all mediatype image). So the seam is NOT unfetched material. THE REAL GAP IS REGISTRATION: only 68 of the 634 held text items are named anywhere in sources.json. Facts drawn from the rest cite the collection-level id, which is defensible but makes item-level provenance uncheckable -- exactly what the read-receipt work exists to prevent. The task is to register the held items individually, prioritising those already cited by facts.
priorities.notes: 2026-08-25 COMPLETE, and it found something larger than itself. The 634-document corpus existed ONLY in the ephemeral scratchpad -- 39 of 634 files were in the repo, and the container is reclaimed after inactivity (f_2320). Copied in and verified by control terms. Then all 566 unregistered items were registered individually: 68-of-634 becomes 634-of-634, 1,300 source records total. Read state set to SKIMMED not extracted, deliberately (f_2321). Byproducts: a 0-byte file exposed an image-only 1900 'Seventh Annual Report of the Current Camp Committee' whose title dates the series to 1894 (f_2322), and its sibling 1900 Junior Camp report was read in full (f_2323).

priorities.description: EDITORIAL DECISION FOR THE OPERATOR: this wiki calls the 1894-1909 camp "Camp Jubilee" across a dozen articles, as though it were the institution's own name. It is not -- every pre-1921 YMCA of Montreal annual report was searched and none uses it; "Jubilee" appears only in the movement's 1844-1894 golden-jubilee sense. The name may still be authentic to camp usage and comes from somewhere (QAHN, the 1951 in-house history, oral tradition). Decide whether to keep it with an attribution, qualify it, or replace it. Renaming a term used across a dozen articles is an editorial call, not a research finding.
priorities.notes: 2026-08-14: evidence assembled and put to the operator. 'Camp Jubilee' appears in exactly ONE of 634 corpus items - the 1988 retrospective - whose 1894 entry is demonstrably wrong in detail (says three islands were PURCHASED in 1894; the 1894-95 report says LEASED, and the 1902 report dates the island auction to 26 Nov 1901). The association's own contemporaneous name was descriptive ('Summer Camp', 'the Summer Camp at Lake St. Joseph'), and the documented proper name for the original site is CAMP OTOREKE, attested from the 1921-22 report. Awaiting the operator's naming decision. MATERIAL UPDATE 2026-08-14: the name is NOT merely a 1988 retrospective coinage -- CONCORDIA'S ARCHIVAL DESCRIPTION of the fonds itself uses it ('P0145/12L - Lac St-Joseph/Camp Jubilee'; 'Season reports of the Junior Camp (Camp Jubilee/Otoreke)'), as does QAHN. It is the received archival/heritage name for the site, with no attestation in the association's own 1894-1909 records. Note also that the camp's own 1935 and 1951 in-house histories do NOT use it. This materially favours KEEPING the name with an attribution over replacing it, since it is the name a researcher would search the Concordia finding aid with. CLOSED 2026-08-14: operator concurs -- keep the name with the explanation. Canonical note added to history/founding-1894.md ('A note on the name'), with short pointers in wiki/README.md, site/camp-otoreke.md and people/billy-ball.md. No articles renamed.

priorities.description: Build the year-by-year attendance series into the wiki. This is the camp's size over 110 years and belongs in a table, probably in timeline-overview.md or a new meta article. SIX INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES must be carried as flags, not smoothed: the 289-boy season is attributed to 1919, 1920 AND 1921 across three reports; 1924 boy-weeks 916 vs 906; 1934 boy-weeks 1,017 vs 972; 1932 campers 360 vs 385; 1965 camper-weeks 1,200 vs 1,182; and the 1930 "increase of 432" does not reconcile with its own series.

priorities.description: Reconcile the scarlet-fever quarantine date. CONVENTION REFINED: the April-to-March change happens at the 1926 report, not 1927; the 1926 report covers an ELEVEN-MONTH transitional period. priorities.description: FIND THE KANAWANA MANUAL OF OPERATIONS (f_2286). NO COPY IS KNOWN TO SURVIVE here. It would be the single best document for 1950s camp operation. priorities.description: OPERATOR DECISION: the repository is PUBLIC, and sources/cache/ is committed to it. That corpus includes the raw OCR of internal camp documents -- among them the 1973 director's report whose Recommendations section names five seasonal staff with negative personal assessments (registered as r_0001). This was committed in an earlier session, not by the p_304 re-read, and it is in git history, so removal means rewriting history and force-pushing, not a delete commit. THREE OPTIONS, all the operator's call: (a) leave it -- the same documents are already public on Internet Archive and the indexed layer is clean, which is where the harm would be; (b) remove sources/cache/ from the repo and history, keeping it locally and in Drive, which costs the reproducibility of every cached citation; (c) make the repository private, which protects the corpus but also takes the wiki off the open web. Recommend (a) plus a note in the repo README explaining what sources/cache/ is, unless the wiki is intended to be a published site, in which case revisit.

priorities.description:
Retrospective sweep for material withheld before the register existed. The p_304 re-read passed over sensitive passages in at least one document before kb/restricted/register.jsonl was created, and the earlier plaque audit and Phase 2 research passes almost certainly did the same without recording it. Re-check the reading ledger (kb/reread/ledger.jsonl) and the research log for anything marked withheld, omitted or 'not extracted', and register each one. Going forward every withholding gets a register entry at the moment it is made.

CONTEXT ESTABLISHED (extraction pass, issues 115-116). The full documentary cycle a 1970s Canadian camp staff record sat inside is now described in the association's own pages, which is the context the embargo policy asks for around r_0001. Barry Lowes, Director of Camp Timberlane and a CCA Task Force member, October 1977: unit or section heads evaluate all staff; a formal sit-down at the end of the first few days; a counsellor self-evaluation at mid-summer on the same form the unit head will use; a final evaluation at the end; and the directors 'collate all of these reports. From them develop lists of repairs, items to be purchased, staff to be rehired, programs to change.' The December 1977 newsletter adds the front end: a STAFF INTERVIEW EVALUATION chart rated one to ten on Appearance, Composure, Maturity, Self-Confidence, Frankness, Leadership Potential and Experience with Children, with the autobiography kept on file. So Robitaille's rehire list is the last step of a nationally recommended procedure, written four years before Lowes set it out. Lowes also states the safeguards that were supposed to come with it -- 'You must be sure to let staff know who will have access to the evaluations. Confidentiality is vital!' and that a subject has 'a right to discuss the report with the person doing them. It is a basic human right and also a sound evaluation technique.' Nothing in the Kanawana document shows whether the people named were ever told.
priorities.notes: The point of the register is that a later pass can see what an earlier one decided not to write down. Entries created retrospectively are worth less than entries created at the time, but they are worth more than nothing.

priorities.description: WIKI UI: decide how embargoed passages are surfaced. The data layer is settled -- embargoed material is held in full in kb/facts.json and written into articles inside <!-- embargo:r_NNNN --> blocks, with kb/restricted/register.jsonl giving the kind, basis and review date for each. What is NOT decided, and should be decided once at the UI layer rather than repeatedly at the collection layer, is what a published edition does with a block: redact the names and keep the passage, replace it with a placeholder naming the register entry and review date, gate it behind a login for researchers, or publish it because the embargo has lapsed. Whichever is chosen, the builder should read the register rather than hard-code dates, so that an embargo lapsing changes the site without changing the articles.
priorities.notes: Reframed 2026-09-03 from a build hook to a design decision, per the operator: 'We need to make surface publication policy decisions at the wiki UI design level, not here.' scripts/build-content.ts is still the boilerplate scaffold it shipped as and is not pointed at wiki/; whatever policy is chosen gets implemented there.

priorities.description: Sampling read of whole Canadian Camping issues, to test what the term list missed. The p_304 pass indexed all 164 issues mechanically and read 664 extracted passages, but the extraction is a term list, and a term list finds only what someone thought to look for -- the failure mode of f_2335 and f_2378. Read six to ten complete issues chosen across the run (early 1950s, mid 1960s, mid 1970s, late 1980s) and record whether anything relevant appears that the terms did not catch. If the sample is clean, the extraction method is validated for the rest of the corpus; if it is not, the term list needs widening and re-running.
priorities.notes: This is the honest complement to a method that traded completeness for tractability, and it is what makes that trade checkable rather than merely asserted.

priorities.description:
The 1972 CCA national songbook. In Fall 1972 Canadian Camping asked every camp in Canada to send in 'the words and list the tune of your camp song so that it can be shared across Canada' for a songbook to be made available to all camps (issue 96 of the word-for-word read). Kanawana was an accredited Quebec camp and a member camp; if it replied, the words AND the tune of a Kanawana camp song were recorded in 1972 -- in the window between the 1941-1945 song books and the modern Marching Song, and the only likely source outside Concordia for a tune attribution. TWO ACTIONS: (1) read forward through the 1973-1976 issues of this run for any announcement, contents list or advertisement for the songbook, and note it in the findings file when found; (2) search externally for a published Canadian Camping Association songbook of the 1970s (Internet Archive, Library and Archives Canada, WorldCat, AbeBooks, Trent University Archives). A SECOND, REAL CANADIAN CAMP SONGBOOK EXISTS AND IS DATED (added 2026-09-04, issue 123). Paul Potter's report on the Nova Scotia Camping Association's 1978 summer project: 'May and June also saw the development of a song book. Although some camps had been working on their own song book, none was large enough to hold all of the songs from every camp. Therefore a PROVINCIAL SONG BOOK WITH MORE THAN FIVE HUNDRED SONGS was published. Since its publication, the book has been in constant demand and may soon require a second printing. The cost is $3.00 and it is available from: Nova Scotia Camping Association, Box 696, Halifax, Nova Scotia B3J 3H5.' This is a findable object: a 1978 provincial camp songbook of 500+ songs, compiled from the repertoires of many camps, published by a CCA member association. Even though it is Nova Scotian rather than Quebec, the Canadian camp song repertoire is largely shared, and a 500-song collection is the best available comparator for identifying which Kanawana songs are house compositions and which are movement-wide. WHERE TO LOOK: the Nova Scotia Camping Association's successor body; Nova Scotia provincial and university libraries; Library and Archives Canada; and Trent (p_312), which collected member-association publications. Note also that the CCA president reported in December 1978 that the NSCA planned to 'put to music' the songbook it had produced. A THIRD SONGBOOK, WITH MUSIC (added 2026-09-04, issue 131): 'Sing with Jack', the first Camp Tawingo Publication, announced in May 1980 -- 'the words and music to 37 favorite camp songs, plus notes for actions by the leader', $4.00 through the CCA Publications Service, by Jack Pearse, then immediate past president of the CCA. Two sequels were announced: 'Campfire Programs with Jack Pearse' and 'Sing (One More Time) with Jack Pearse'. Unlike the Nova Scotia collection this one carries MUSIC as well as words, which makes it the better comparator for identifying tunes. Camp Tawingo still operates, so its own publications office is the first place to ask. BOTH SONGBOOKS NOW HAVE FULL CATALOGUE ENTRIES (added 2026-09-04, issue 134). The CCA's own bilingual publications catalogue of December 1980 lists them: (1) '*COME ON ... LET'S SING* -- Nova Scotia Camping Association, 156p, 1979, $3.75. Words to 583 favorite camp songs compiled by the N.S.C.A.' -- a title, publisher, year, page count, price and song count for the provincial collection first reported at issue 123, and 583 songs rather than the 'more than five hundred' of the original notice. Search library catalogues for 'Come On Let's Sing' with the NSCA as author. (2) '*SING WITH JACK PEARSE* -- J. Pearse, 37p, Camp Tawingo Publications, 1980, $4.00. 31 songs with music, delightfully illustrated, many actions included' -- so 37 PAGES and 31 SONGS, correcting the May 1980 announcement's '37 songs'. A sequel, 'Sing (One More Time) with Jack Pearse', was due early 1981. Also in the catalogue: 'Sing!', ed. ACA Publications Committee, 95p, World Around Songs, revised 1978, words and music; 'Tent and Trail Songs', 80p, World Around Songs, 1966, 116 songs to supplement Sing!; and J. Tobitt's 'A Counselor's Guide to Camp Singing', ACA 1971. Between them these five books are the printed repertoire a Canadian camp of 1980 could buy, and the comparison set for deciding which Kanawana songs are house compositions.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 123): A REAL CANADIAN CAMP SONGBOOK EXISTS, DATED AND ADDRESSED. Paul Potter's report on the Nova Scotia Camping Association's 1978 summer project: 'a provincial song book with more than five hundred songs was published. Since its publication, the book has been in constant demand and may soon require a second printing. The cost is $3.00 and it is available from: Nova Scotia Camping Association, Box 696, Halifax, Nova Scotia B3J 3H5.' Five hundred songs compiled from the repertoires of every camp in a province. It is Nova Scotian rather than Quebec, but the Canadian camp song repertoire is largely shared, and a collection that size is the best available instrument for deciding which Kanawana songs are house compositions and which are movement-wide -- the question traditions/camp-songs-cheers.md cannot currently answer. Ask the NSCA's successor body, Nova Scotian public and university libraries, LAC and Trent. Two related items from the same years: the CCA's Skill School Project planned a national SONGLEADING instructors' school for 1979, and Tolbitt's Counsellor's Guide to Camp Singing (44 pp.) was in the CCA catalogue from 1975.

THE NOVA SCOTIA BOOK NOW HAS A TITLE (extraction pass, issue 134). The CCA's December 1980 catalogue lists it: 'COME ON ... LET'S SING -- Nova Scotia Camping Association, 156p, 1979, $3.75. Words to 583 favorite camp songs compiled by the N.S.C.A.' Searchable in library catalogues by that title. The same catalogue corrects the Tawingo book: 'SING WITH JACK PEARSE -- J. Pearse, 37p, Camp Tawingo Publications, 1980 -- 31 songs WITH MUSIC.' Words only in the Nova Scotia book, tunes in the Tawingo one, so both are wanted for different reasons. The full 1980 printed repertoire also includes Sing! (ACA/World Around Songs, revised 1978, words and music), Tent and Trail Songs (116 songs, 1966) and Tobitt's A Counselor's Guide to Camp Singing.
priorities.notes: Feeds p_045-adjacent song threads and p_048 directly. Source: Canadian Camping Vol. 25 No. 1 (Fall 1972), p. 3. Nova Scotia songbook recorded at issue 123 (Canadian Camping Vol. 31 No. 1, February 1979, p. 6) and issue 122.

priorities.description:
[ANSWERED 2026-09-04 -- destination confirmed as TRENT, superseding the earlier Waterloo note] Locate the C.C.A. Archives. The Fall 1972 notice asked every camp director to send the CCA office 'two copies of your camp brochure -- they are needed for the C.C.A. Archives and for display at the February Conference at Geneva Park.' The Summer 1973 issue reported that a new ARCHIVES committee was to gather material 'to be housed at THE UNIVERSITY OF WATERLOO' -- but that was the 1973 plan, not the outcome. Adele Ebbs, chairman of the CCA Archives Committee, writing in October 1976: 'In 1967 official collecting and sorting of camping records was started by a small group... We have been fortunate in finding a home for our Canadian Camping Archives at Trent University in Peterborough. Their Department of Canadian Studies is very supportive of our efforts... Such national papers belong at Trent.' Material was to be sent to 'Mr Kenneth Johnson, Archivist, Trent University, Peterborough, Ontario K9J 7B8', with the CCA paying delivery costs. The founding deposit was F.M. Van Wagner's own papers ('The first and very valuable contribution of papers came from F.M. Van Wagner who was C.C.A. President 1958-60'). The Archives Committee was constituted with a representative from each provincial association. NEXT ACTION: query Trent University Archives for the Canadian Camping Association fonds and for camp brochures collected from member camps in the 1970s -- a Kanawana brochure of the early 1970s is exactly the kind of item the 1972 solicitation was designed to collect. Trent already holds the OCA deposit (22 October 1970) and the Mary S. Edgar fonds, so one enquiry covers three collections. RESIDUAL CHECK ONLY: ask Waterloo Special Collections whether a first tranche was deposited there in 1973-75 and never transferred. ALSO ASK TRENT FOR (added 2026-09-04, issue 111): Sharon Brown's CCA bibliography of 'all books, catalogues, papers, magazines etc. which would be of any interest to anyone in the camping and related fields', announced in February 1977 as due mid-April 1977. If it survives it is a finding aid for the whole field, compiled by the association whose archive is at Trent. Ask also for the CCA Publications Committee records of Punch Jackson's book service of the same period. TWO NAMED CONFERENCE REPORTS TO ASK FOR (added 2026-09-04, issue 124): the CCA stated in March 1979 that 'the content of each Conference is gathered together and each of these reports may be obtained through the Publications Committee at the National Office', naming the FRENCH LANGUAGE CAMPING CONFERENCE (1976) -- the first in Canada, chaired by Abbe Paul Belanger at the Montmorency Forest -- and the OUTDOOR EDUCATION CONFERENCE (1974). Both were purchasable documents in 1979 and are exactly the sort of association publication the archive collected. Ask also for the Woodsmanship Instructor's Manual (bilingual, in preparation 1979) and the reports of the Geneva Park national conferences. NOTE the Archives chairmanship passed from Adele Ebbs to HELEN STEWART by March 1979 -- a second name to cite when writing to Trent. PROVENANCE NOTE (added 2026-09-04, issue 131): the scanned copies this project is reading came from Trent itself. The mailing label on the back page of the May 1980 issue reads 'Trent University, Archives Dept., Peterborough, Attention: K. Johnson' -- the archivist Adele Ebbs named in 1976. The Internet Archive run of Canadian Camping is Trent's own deposit copy, which both corroborates the Trent story and means the association's other publications very likely went to the same address by the same route.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 109): THE ARCHIVIST IS NAMED. Adele Ebbs gives the address to write to -- 'Mr Kenneth Johnson, Archivist, Trent University, Peterborough, Ontario K9J 7B8' -- says the Canadian Camping Archives Committee was established in 1975 with representatives from each province, dates the start of official collecting to 1967, and states that 'The Archives at Trent are National'. The founding deposit was F. M. Van Wagner's papers (see p_317).

TWO MORE ITEMS FOR THE SAME ENQUIRY (extraction pass, issues 111 and 113). (a) Sharon Brown was compiling for the CCA, due mid-April 1977, 'a complete bibliography of all books, catalogues, papers, magazines etc. which would be of any interest to anyone in the camping and related fields' -- a finding aid for this whole field if it survives. (b) The 1977 Task Force report on the CCA's future, chaired by John Latimer, was distributed so that 'the full report along with all of the background material is available in every Provincial Association office,' which means a copy went to the Quebec office. Ask Trent for both by name.

THREE MORE NAMED PUBLICATIONS FOR THE SAME ENQUIRY (extraction pass, issues 124 and 127). (a) The reports of the FRENCH LANGUAGE CAMPING CONFERENCE (1976) and the OUTDOOR EDUCATION CONFERENCE (1974), which the March 1979 issue says 'may be obtained through the Publications Committee at the National Office' -- the 1976 one being the first French-language camping conference in Canada. (b) Kirk Wipper's WOODSMANSHIP LEADERS' GUIDE (CCA, 1979, 155 pp., $6.00, loose-leaf), translated into French by Rosaire Corbin. Also note that ARCHIVES passed from Adele Ebbs to HELEN STEWART for 1978-79, so Stewart is a second name to ask Trent about.

PROVENANCE NOTE (extraction pass, issue 131): THE SCANS THIS PROJECT READS CAME FROM TRENT. The mailing label on the back page of Vol. 32 No. 3 (May 1980) reads 'Trent University, Archives Dept., Peterborough, Attention: K. Johnson' -- the archivist Adele Ebbs named in October 1976. The Internet Archive run of Canadian Camping is Trent's own deposit copy, addressed to the man who received the Canadian Camping Archives. That corroborates the Trent story from the physical object, and means the association's OTHER publications very likely reached the same address by the same route -- the conference reports, the Woodsmanship Leaders' Guide, the tabulated tripping survey, the songbooks. Ask for the whole accession, not for titles one at a time.
priorities.notes: Sources: Canadian Camping Vol. 25 No. 1 (Fall 1972), p. 3; Vol. 25 No. 4 (Summer 1973), p. 2; Adele Ebbs, 'Canadian Camping Archives', Canadian Camping Vol. 28 No. 4 (October 1976). Found by the word-for-word read, issues 96, 99 and 109. The Waterloo destination recorded at issue 99 was superseded by the Trent statement at issue 109; block 99 of cc_findings.md has been patched in place to say so.

priorities.description: Jack Pearse's national camping history committee, 1972. Canadian Camping Fall 1972 reports that 'Jack Pearse is working on the establishment of a committee to investigate ways and means of gathering together material which can be compiled into a master document on the history of the camping movement in Canada.' Whatever that committee produced -- or failed to produce -- is the natural place for a national account in which Kanawana, as one of the oldest camps in Canada, would appear. Track it forward through the run, then search externally for any resulting publication.
priorities.notes: Source: Canadian Camping Vol. 25 No. 1 (Fall 1972), 'Have You Heard? Do You Know?', p. 13.

priorities.description: THE ANNUAL QUEBEC ACCREDITATION REPORTS ON KANAWANA. John Hasell, chairman of the CCA National Standards Committee, states in the January 1975 Directory Issue that 'some provinces requir[e] a visit every two or three years, but Quebec has developed its programme to the point where every camp is re-accredited annually' -- printed in both languages. Kanawana was an accredited Quebec camp; Alta Kahn dates Quebec accreditation to the pioneer years of 1959-60. So what is missing is not one report but A SERIES: an annual, itemised, externally written assessment of Kanawana's administration, personnel practices, site, programme, health and safety, running from about 1960. Hasell lists what each visitation examined; Madelene Allen of Camp Ouareau (issue 101) describes a visitation in practice, including a written MARKING SCHEME. WHERE TO ASK, in order: (1) the QCA English Section's own Archives -- the same directory names Mr. Joseph A. Hood as Archives committee chairman in 1975; (2) the successor body, the Association des camps du Quebec, at its Montreal office; (3) Concordia's YMCA of Montreal fonds, since the camp would have kept its own copies; (4) BAnQ, for a body incorporated under Quebec law. ASK TRENT FIRST (added 2026-09-04, issue 118). The project already knows of a QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION FONDS AT TRENT UNIVERSITY, 85-013, covering 1948-1982 -- cited as source 23 of connections/related-camps/quebec-camp-landscape.md and never queried for accreditation records. That date range covers the entire accreditation era this priority is about, and Adele Ebbs confirms Trent is where the national and provincial camping papers were being gathered (p_312). The word-for-word read has since shown exactly what that fonds should contain: the QCA English Section executive met monthly at the MONTREAL YMCA (13 February, 13 March, 10 April, 8 May, 12 June 1978), held general meetings, an annual conference, a Counsellor Conference and a STANDARDS MEETING (7 June 1978), and the joint ACQ-QCA Provincial Council met separately. Minutes of the QCA Standards Committee are the specific target. NOTE ALSO a corroborating detail from Eanswythe Flynn's May 1978 director's checklist -- 'Find out from your provincial camping association whether or not THIS IS YOUR YEAR for a Standards Visitation' -- which is written for an Ontario readership on a multi-year cycle and independently confirms that Quebec's annual re-accreditation was exceptional, not the norm. ONE MORE ACQ DOCUMENT TO ASK FOR (added 2026-09-04, issue 129): the ACQ's 'formateurs-multiplicateurs' Director Education Program, prepared February 1976 and serialised in Canadian Camping from February 1980, refers to a standard interview sheet -- 'un formulaire est necessaire pour obtenir les renseignements utiles... (cf. feuille A.C.Q.)'. A provincial association's own staff-selection form, dated to the exact period of Kanawana's thinnest records, and issued to its member camps. Ask the ACQ successor body and Trent for the programme and the form together.
priorities.notes: Sources: Canadian Camping Vol. 27 No. 2 (January 1975), Hasell 'Standards for Camps' pp. 20-21 and QCA English Section officer list; Vol. 26 No. 1 (Fall 1973) for Kahn; Vol. 26 No. 2 (Winter/Spring 1974) for Allen. Word-for-word read, issues 100, 101, 103. Extended at issue 118 (Canadian Camping Vol. 30 No. 2, April 1978) and issue 117 (Vol. 30 No. 1, February 1978, the 1978 calendar). The Trent QCA fonds 85-013 pointer comes from the project's own existing source list, not from the magazine.

priorities.description: THE NATIONAL YMCA CAMP DIRECTORY, c.1975. The back page of the January 1975 Canadian Camping Directory Issue advertises a 'DIRECTORY OF YMCA/YM-YWCA/YWCA RESIDENCE CAMPS IN CANADA -- to be available soon at all Y's', from the National Council, YMCA of Canada, 2160 Yonge Street, Toronto M4S 2A9, and the YWCA of Canada, 571 Jarvis Street, Toronto M4Y 2J1. A national directory of YMCA residence camps, published about 1975, in which Kanawana would necessarily appear -- a separate publication from the CCA's. ACTIONS: search Library and Archives Canada, the YMCA Canada national archives, University of Minnesota's Kautz Family YMCA Archives (which holds Canadian material), WorldCat and the Internet Archive for a mid-1970s YMCA of Canada camp directory. A YMCA-published entry would give the camp's own description of itself rather than the association's summary.
priorities.notes: Source: Canadian Camping Vol. 27 No. 2 (January 1975), back page advertisement. Word-for-word read, issue 103.

priorities.description: KANAWANA'S 1975 SEASON AND FEES, recoverable from the page image. The Quebec table in the January 1975 Directory Issue carries a SEASON/FEES column, but the cached OCR renders it as a floating block of dates and prices detached from their rows, so Kanawana's season dates and fee CANNOT be safely attributed from the text. They are on the printed page. ACTION: fetch the page images for this issue from the Internet Archive item and read the Kanawana row directly. The same fetch would settle the three single-character column codes ('X X C') whose headers the OCR mangles, and recover the fee for Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye. Low effort, high certainty.
priorities.notes: Source: Canadian Camping Vol. 27 No. 2 (January 1975), Quebec accredited member camps table. Word-for-word read, issue 103.

priorities.description:
FIND VAN WAGNER'S 1955 MANUAL OF STANDARDS. The April 1975 tribute to F.M. Van Wagner states that 'In 1955 he formulated and first introduced a Manual of Standards for children's summer camps in the Province of Quebec.' That is the origin document of the standards Kanawana was accredited against, with an author and a year. The sequence is now continuous: manual 1955 -> accreditation 'in the pioneer stage' 1959-60 under Alta Kahn -> provincial incorporation 23 January 1961 -> annual re-accreditation of every Quebec camp by 1975. WHERE TO LOOK -- FIRST: the F.M. VAN WAGNER PAPERS AT TRENT. Adele Ebbs (October 1976) reports that Van Wagner's own papers were the founding deposit of the Canadian Camping Archives at Trent University, Department of Canadian Studies -- 'from these papers we have many records of the early days of our Association.' A manual he authored is precisely the kind of document that would travel with his papers, and this is now the single most likely location. THEN: the QCA/ACQ successor body; the Camp Nominingue archive (Van Wagner founded and ran it 1925 onward, and Nominingue is still operating); BAnQ; Concordia's YMCA of Montreal fonds, since an accredited camp would hold a copy; and Trent, alongside the OCA deposit. Note also that Van Wagner was CCA president 'with Office in Montreal from 1958 to 1961' -- the national office was in Montreal for three years, and its records of that period are a separate target.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 109): LOOK IN THE VAN WAGNER PAPERS AT TRENT FIRST. Adele Ebbs, writing as chairman of the CCA Archives Committee in October 1976: 'The first and very valuable contribution of papers came from F.M. Van Wagner who was C.C.A. President 1958-60. From these papers we have many records of the early days of our Association.' Van Wagner founded the Quebec Camping Association in 1937 and was its first president, wrote the 1955 Manual, and was CCA president with the national office in Montreal. His own papers were the founding deposit of the national camping archive at Trent, so the Manual and early QCA records are more likely to be there than anywhere else this project has considered. Ask Trent for the Van Wagner papers by name, alongside the OCA deposit of October 1970 and the Mary S. Edgar fonds -- three separate camping deposits at one institution.
priorities.notes: Source: Frances M. Kelly, 'A Tribute to Q.C.A.'s Mr. Van', Canadian Camping Vol. 27 No. 3 (April 1975), p. 11-12. Word-for-word read, issue 104. Feeds p_314. Sharpened 2026-09-04 at issue 109: Van Wagner's papers are the founding deposit of the CCA archive at Trent, so p_317 and p_312 should be pursued in the same enquiry.

priorities.description: FIND COUSINEAU'S 'HEBERTISME' BOOKLET (1975). The November 1975 Canadian Camping newsletter advertises: 'HEBERTISME -- a new booklet written by Claude Cousineau and published by the Ontario Ministry of Culture and Recreation. 50 cents each from: Ontario Government Publications Service, 3 B-7 Macdonald Block, Queen's Park, Toronto.' This is the document that would settle the open conflict on Hebert's own dates: Cousineau (issue 82) has a pre-war methode naturelle demonstrated in 1913, brought to Quebec after the Second World War by Father Raoul Cloutier and Georges Gauvreau; Walter Mingie (issue 94) has Hebert training the French navy DURING the First World War. Cousineau wrote one side of that conflict and here sets it out at length for a government publisher. SEARCH: Ontario government publications 1975, Library and Archives Canada, University of Ottawa (where Cousineau taught in the School of Physical Education and Recreation / Departement de Recreologie), WorldCat, and the Ontario Ministry of Culture and Recreation's publication lists. Bears on wiki/traditions/programs-activities.md, which carries the hebertisme paragraph. SECOND DOCUMENT ADDED 2026-09-04 (issue 110): the Alberta Camping Association announced a 'Practical Guide to Hebertism', produced out of the experience of three Alberta camps funded in 1976 by the provincial Department of Recreation and Parks to set up hebertisme courses. As a government-funded provincial publication it may be easier to locate than Cousineau's booklet -- try the Alberta Camping Association successor body, Alberta provincial government publication catalogues, and university libraries in Alberta. New Brunswick reported in October 1976 that hebertisme 'continues to grow in many camps... due to the tremendous influence of Claude Cousineau's book on the subject', so the method was demonstrably travelling across the country within a year of publication. DATING NOTE (added 2026-09-04, issue 120): the CCA's June 1978 publications catalogue lists the Alberta Camping Association's 'Director's Guide for Counsellor Training' at $3.00 as a published Canadian book, but does NOT list the 'Practical Guide to Hebertism'. So as of June 1978 the hebertisme guide had not yet appeared -- do not assume a 1977 imprint when searching library catalogues; look from 1978 onward.
priorities.notes: Source: Canadian Camping Vol. 28 No. 1 (November 1975), p. 4 notice. Word-for-word read, issue 106. Extended at issue 110 (Canadian Camping Vol. 28 No. 5, December 1976, p. 4).

priorities.description:
TRACE THE 1976 NATIONAL ORAL-BIOGRAPHY PROJECT -- and check whether a Quebec tape covers Kanawana. Adele Ebbs, October 1976: 'At the Quebec Board meeting last spring a long list of camp pioneers was drawn up and agreement was reached by the Provincial Presidents that their associations would start taping oral biographies of those people.' Tapes were to go to Trent, where 'The Trent Archivist will make a copy and return the original.' This means (a) a list of Canadian camp pioneers was compiled at a CCA board meeting held in Quebec in spring 1976, and (b) the Quebec Camping Association undertook to tape its own pioneers. Anyone who ran or shaped Kanawana before 1976 -- and F.M. Van Wagner, who wrote Quebec's standards -- is a candidate to be on that list or on a tape. NEXT ACTION: ask Trent Archives for the CCA oral history tapes, the pioneer list itself, and any accession from the Quebec/ACQ association; ask the QCA successor body whether its tapes survive locally, since only copies went to Trent. A recording of a Quebec camp pioneer speaking in 1976-77 would be the earliest oral-history material this project could reach. SECONDARY VALUE: this is a direct 1976 precedent for the project's own pending DRAFT_ORAL_HISTORY_INSTRUMENT -- if the CCA's interview guidance survives with the tapes, it is worth reading before drafting ours. THE PROJECT HAD A NAMED CHAIRMAN (added 2026-09-04, issue 116): the CCA's list of committees and projects for 1977-78 includes 'PROJECTS -- Oral History -- Jay Haddad -- Ontario'. So the taping agreed at the Quebec board meeting in spring 1976 became a standing national project with a chairman by the winter of 1977-78. Haddad also sat on the CCA Task Force that reported in April 1977. ASK FOR: Haddad's oral history project files, correspondence and tape list, at Trent alongside the CCA fonds; and search for Jay Haddad himself (Ontario camping, 1970s) for a personal deposit or an obituary naming the project. A SECOND TAPE SERIES EXISTS (added 2026-09-04, issue 119): the CCA sold audio cassettes of its National Leadership Development Conference at Geneva Park, 19-22 January 1978 -- eighteen sessions at $3.50 each, ordered from M. Lee, R.R. No. 1, Port Sydney, Ontario. The published titles and speakers are: Selecting a Site (Ruth Mowat); Finance and Legislation (Ron Johnstone); Effective Administration (Ken Willis); Conserve Society (Craig Copeland); Maintenance and Building (Wilf Jackson, of Catholic Community Services Montreal); There's More to P.R. (Punch Jackson); Help a Child Grow (Gordon Jasper); Expectations (Bruno Morawetz); To Whom Directors Answer (Shanley Parkinson); Human Climate in Camp (Jean Funk); Will Staff Return (Bob Slingerland); Needs of Children (Patterson and Owen); High A.Q. Programs (Mayotte and Delainey); Program Models (Elaine King); Developing a Nature Program (Bob Cameron); Developing Programme Goals (Lorne Bowering); Year Around Programme Ideals (Ted Yard); New Program Ideas (Austin Matthews). This is a dated, itemised 1978 recording of Canadian camp directors talking about their work -- distinct from the pioneer oral biographies, and worth asking Trent for by conference name. THE PROJECT WAS FOLDED INTO ARCHIVES (added 2026-09-04, issue 129). By February 1980 the CCA's committee list reads 'Archives and Oral History -- Miss Helen Stewart': the separate Oral History project under Jay Haddad has been merged with the Archives committee under a single chairman. That simplifies the search -- the tapes and the pioneer list should be wherever the Archives committee's material went, which Adele Ebbs states was Trent (p_312). Ask Trent for the Archives committee's accessions of 1976-1980 as one body, under Ebbs, Stewart and Haddad's names together, rather than for an oral history collection by that name. THE ARCHIVE HAS A NAMED ARCHIVIST AND A PUBLISHED INVITATION (added 2026-09-04, issue 140): Canadian Camping Vol. 33 No. 6 (Winter 1982), p. 5, prints the association's own notice -- 'The CCA/ACC Archives are located at Trent University. The Oral History Interview Tapes reflect the efforts of many volunteers to record the history of the camping movement in Canada. Anyone wishing further information on the CCA/ACC Archives should communicate his specific area of interest to: Mr. Ken Johnson, Archivist, Thomas J. Bata Library, Trent University, Peterborough, Ontario K9J 7B8, (705) 748-1413.' That is the same K. Johnson to whom the May 1980 issue in this run was addressed (issue 131), which also confirms that the scans being read are Trent's own deposit copies. The association's instruction is to write in with a SPECIFIC AREA OF INTEREST, so the request should name Quebec, the Association des Camps du Quebec, the Quebec Camping Association English Section, the YMCA of Montreal, and Kanawana. CRITICALLY: the Charles Plewman interview printed in that same issue (Jay Haddad, 15 August 1976) is an EXCERPT -- 'the following are excerpts from that interview'. So the tape series holds full interviews of which the magazine printed only parts, and the request must ask for the recordings and any transcripts, not only for what was printed. Also ask whether the association's minutes are in the same fonds, since they bear on conflict c_029 (the Ottawa/Toronto disagreement about where the CCA was founded). THREE NAMED DOCUMENTS TO ASK FOR (added 2026-09-04, issue 142). The CCA/ACC Archives Committee's annual report for 1981-82 (Canadian Camping Vol. 34 No. 2, Summer 1982, p. 9; the chairman named three months earlier is Eileen Mayotte of Saskatchewan) records that it circulated three things to every provincial association, Quebec included: (1) a SAMPLE QUESTIONNAIRE ON CAMP ARCHIVES, sent to all provincial presidents in May 1981, which several provinces used -- this is the form on which a Quebec answer would have been written; (2) the oral-history taping 'GUIDELINES FOR INTERVIEWS', DEVELOPED BY THE OCA ARCHIVES COMMITTEE -- exactly the instrument this priority says should be read before the project drafts its own oral-history interview instrument, and it may be easier to obtain from the Ontario Camping Association's successor than from Trent; and (3) the 'FINDING AID FOR CCA/ACC ARCHIVES' stored at Trent University, forwarded to each province -- so a catalogue of the Trent holdings exists in multiple copies and should be requested by that title before any blind enquiry. Ask Trent for all three, and ask the OCA separately for the interview guidelines. AND ASK FOR THE 1982 'CATCH UP WITH YOUR PAST' RETURNS (added 2026-09-04, issue 143). Canadian Camping Vol. 34 No. 3 (Autumn 1982), p. 9, prints a boxed appeal over Ken Johnson's name at Trent: 'Children's camping is older than most of us realize. In time for the coming International Camping Congress and for our own information, we need to know WHO OPENED THE FIRST CAMP IN CANADA. As well, we would like to co-ordinate A LIST OF CAMPS IN CANADA WHICH WERE OPENED PRIOR TO 1900, 1910, AND 1920. Please dig into provincial government departments (education, health, land titles/surveys) as well as those of Church, YWCA, YMCA, Boy Scouts, Girl Guides, CGIT, and private records. This kind of information has never been researched in detail.' KANAWANA DATES ITSELF FROM 1894 AND BELONGS ON THE PRE-1900 LIST, so if the Quebec association or the YMCA of Montreal answered, an independent 1982 statement of the camp's founding date went to Trent -- and the compilation, gathered for the January 1983 Congress, would sit with the Congress papers in the same fonds. ASK FOR: the returns, any compiled list, and any correspondence with Quebec. Note also that the search list the CCA gave its members is a good checklist for Kanawana's own pre-1900 record in its own right: provincial education, health, and land titles/survey departments. UPDATE 2026-09-04 (issue 147, the 1982 Annual Report insert): the Archives Committee report for 1982-83, signed BRUNO MORAWETZ, Ph.D. -- a new chairman's name, and the same Bruno Morawetz who directed Camp Ponacka and wrote the 1975 'annual Hoax' article -- is the fullest account of CCA archival practice this read has found, and it changes where to look. (1) Provincial associations were told in the plainest terms to 'send all materials relating to the business of the Provincial Association to the CCA office for DEPOSIT AT TRENT UNIVERSITY', so anything the Quebec association or the ACQ sent after January 1983 is at Trent and not in Quebec -- ask Trent for Quebec provincial association material by name. (2) BERNADINE DODGE is named alongside Helen Stewart and Ken Johnston [Johnson] as having built the Congress Archives Room display; add her to the Trent enquiry. (3) A PHOTOGRAPHIC RECORD OF ALL FORMER CCA PRESIDENTS was prepared in January 1983, 'consisting of two frames with empty spaces for the next five CCA Presidents' -- a discrete, findable object that should be in the fonds and that would picture the Quebec presidents. (4) The Archives Room also held exhibits from the KANAWA MUSEUM provided by Professor Kirk Wipper, assisted by EANSWYTHE FLYNN -- a second new name. (5) Explicit null: six provincial associations sent slide carousels of camp scenes (Newfoundland, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Ontario, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia); QUEBEC IS NOT AMONG THEM, nor Alberta nor B.C. (6) Separately, Janet Adamson's Ontario report states that 1983 was the OCA's 50th anniversary and that 'the Archives Committee is publishing a booklet of the OCA's history to commemorate this anniversary. This will be available in the Autumn.' A 1983 OCA HISTORY BOOKLET therefore exists -- written by the association whose own 1930-33 founding date this project has three competing versions of, and by the archives committee that would know. Find it: Trent, the OCA itself, Ontario library catalogues, AMICUS/Voila, WorldCat. UPDATE 2026-09-04 (issue 148): THE TRENT ARCHIVIST IS NAMED WITH AN ADDRESS. Bruno Morawetz's Archives Update in Autumn 1983: 'We have a new archivist working on our collection at Trent University. Congratulations to Mrs. BERNADINE DODGE on her recent appointment at Trent. Interested members may contact Bernadine Dodge at: BATA LIBRARY, TRENT UNIVERSITY, PETERBOROUGH, ONTARIO K9L 7B8.' So the CCA fonds had a named professional custodian from 1983; any finding aid for the collection was made under her; and her own later career at Trent is traceable, which is a way into the collection's history if the fonds description is thin. Morawetz also renews the deposit instruction in a narrower and more useful form -- 'now is the time to send copies of last year's CONFERENCE PROGRAMS to the CCA Archives c/o the National Office' -- so provincial and camp conference programmes, Quebec's included, were actively solicited into the fonds in 1983-84. And Cliff Labbett, Immediate Past President, was in autumn 1983 'canvassing all the CCA Past Presidents for ideas to celebrate CCA's 50th Anniversary in 1986', which means (a) a 1986 anniversary publication or event may exist and be findable, and (b) correspondence with every living past president was generated in 1983-84 and should be in the fonds. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 150): THE OCA HISTORY IS PUBLISHED AND NAMED. It is 'BLUE LAKE AND ROCKY SHORE', 112 pages, illustrated, written by a committee of OCA executive members, published by NATURAL HERITAGE of Toronto ((416) 694-7907 in 1984), launched at the OCA annual conference at the Inn On The Park, Toronto, 23-25 February 1984, and sold through the CCA Bookstore at $8.95. Order it or find it: Natural Heritage / Natural Heritage Books (later an imprint of Dundurn), Ontario library catalogues, AMICUS/Voila, WorldCat, abebooks. The magazine reviewed it as the first history of Canadian children's camping ever written, covering the turn of the century onward, so it is a secondary source on the whole movement and not only on Ontario -- and it is ten years earlier than any Kanawana centennial material. Note for the founding-date question: the review says only that the OCA was 'founded in the early Thirties', which does not discriminate between 1930, 1932 and 1933. ALSO from this issue: the NEATHERN TRUST is now sized and dated -- a $10,000 grant to the CCA announced spring 1984, instigated by Dr. Mary L. Northway, principal and interest to be expended after ten years, for simple outdoor living, understanding of the natural world, and conservation/energy education. Its projects therefore run 1984-1994. Northway's own camp biography is given: camper then staff at Glen Bernard Camp, Sundridge, 1922-1939; co-founder with Flora Morrison of Windy Pine, a tripping camp near Minden, in 1940. Her papers and the trust's records are worth the same enquiry as the CCA fonds. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 151): TRENT HOLDS TRANSCRIBED ORAL HISTORIES -- stated outright for the first time in this run. Adele and Harry Ebbs's 1984 tribute to C. R. 'Blackie' Blackstock prints several hundred words of his speech and says: 'The following quotes are excerpts from the CAMPING ARCHIVES AT TRENT UNIVERSITY.' So the collection contains interview transcripts, not only institutional paper, and the Jay Haddad interview series this project has relied on (Plewman 1976, May Brown 1976, Latimer 1982, Booth 1982) may survive there in fuller form than the edited magazine versions. ASK TRENT FOR THE INTERVIEW/ORAL HISTORY SERIES BY NAME. Also: Bruno Morawetz's 1983 archives report describes HOW provincial material arrives -- 'each Provincial Association was sent a large brown envelope marked "Archives"... for mailing at a later date when the envelope is about to burst' -- so Quebec deposits, if any, arrive as irregular bulk envelopes rather than ordered transfers, and may be uncatalogued. Archivist address restated as Bernadine Dodge, Trent University, Peterborough K9J 7B8 (issue 148 gave K9L 7B8; OCR variance, check both). And Clifford Labbett's 50th Anniversary Task Force lists five candidate 1986 activities -- kite flying across Canada; participation in the July 1st celebrations in Ottawa; a National Camping Day tie-in with private-industry sponsorship; official UNESCO recognition for camping's contribution to environmental protection; and across-Canada campfires -- any of which would have generated 1986 paper reaching member camps. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 152): A NATIONAL TAPING INSTRUCTION, AND A CALL FOR PROVINCIAL HISTORIES. Bruno Morawetz's 'Are You Taping Your Leaders?' (Autumn 1984), crediting the inspiration of HELEN STEWART, the Ontario Archives Chairman, tells every provincial association: 'make use of TAPE RECORDERS to tape interviews with individual Camp Directors and to tape addresses that are given at conferences and workshops... send copies to the CCA Archives at Trent University, Peterborough, if it is of national importance.' Taken with issue 151's statement that the Blackstock quotations are 'excerpts from the Camping Archives at Trent University', it is near-certain the Trent collection holds SOUND RECORDINGS as well as paper, accumulating from 1984 onward. ASK TRENT FOR AUDIO / ORAL HISTORY RECORDINGS BY THAT DESCRIPTION, not only for files. Second: 'The Ontario Archives Committee has just finished writing the history of the Ontario Camping Association... and IT IS HOPED THAT OTHER PROVINCES WILL START THINKING ABOUT THE WRITING OF THEIR OWN HISTORIES.' So provincial associations were formally urged in 1984 to write their own histories -- ASK WHETHER THE ACQ OR THE QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION EVER DID, and if so when and by whom; a Quebec equivalent of Blue Lake and Rocky Shore would be a major secondary source for Kanawana. Also from the same issue: the editor's own list of the complete interview series he published -- CHARLES PLEWMAN, JUNE LABBETT, MAY BROWN, JOHN LATIMER, MARJORIE BOOTH and LEO BUSCAGLIA -- which is the exact set to ask Trent for in unedited form. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 153): 1985 IS THE YEAR TO LOOK FOR KANAWANA HERITAGE MATERIAL. Three separate national prompts to Canadian camps to write down their own history all land in 1985: (a) the CCA's International Youth Year 'National Celebration Event' of August 1985, for which every member camp was to receive programme kits on fitness, environment, PEACE and HISTORICAL ROOTS (issue 151); (b) Bruno Morawetz's instruction to provincial associations to tape interviews with camp directors and conference addresses for deposit at Trent (issue 152); and (c) HERITAGE YEAR 1985, marking a century since land was set aside near Banff, for which the Winter 1985 issue printed seventy-plus bilingual suggestions including 'RECORD THE ORAL HISTORY OF YOUR COMMUNITY ON AUDIO OR VIDEO TAPE by interviewing senior citizens and local historians', 'produce an historical atlas of your community', 'produce an historic newspaper', and 'compare the local natural environment with various periods in the past, using archives, oral histories, wildlife and bird counts'. If Kanawana ever generated heritage or oral-history material outside its annual reports, 1985 is the single most likely year, and it falls squarely inside the 1980-1986 period for which no Kanawana season report survives. ALSO from this issue, and important for the project's own record-keeping: Fitness Canada withdrew funding for the CCA executive director's post at the end of November 1984 and cut all management support by 33-1/3% a year to terminate in 1988 -- which is why Canadian Camping stops in 1988. That belongs in meta/sources-index.md as the explanation of this source's end date. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 154) -- THE SINGLE MOST CONCRETE 1980s ASK. The International Youth Year kit was not a vague plan: 'The Canadian Camping Association will provide each member camp with a kit of program material... The kit will be DIRECTLY MAILED TO EACH CAMP IN EARLY MAY [1985].' Its contents are credited by author, and the first is 'HISTORICAL ROOTS ACTIVITIES - DR. BRUNO MORAWETZ, CAMP PONACKA' -- written by the CCA's own archives chairman. Others: Environmental Activities (Mike Walters, Camp Chief Hector); Fitness Activities (Fitness Canada); Peace Activities (Canadian Peace Congress); IYY Campfire Program (Jack Pearse, Jane McCutcheon, John Jorgenson, Camp Tawingo). The National Celebration Event was WEDNESDAY 24 JULY 1985 and every camp was asked at minimum to run the common campfire programme. ASK TRENT FOR THE 1985 IYY KIT BY NAME, and for Morawetz's Historical Roots Activities specifically -- it is a named document by a named author, mailed to Kanawana, inside the 1980-1986 window for which no Kanawana season report survives. The national co-ordinator was Ian Fowler, 100 Westmorland Street, Moncton, N.B.; the Quebec member of the task force was PETER GODDARD OF MONTREAL. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 157): A SECOND NATIONAL HISTORY PROMPT, AND THIS ONE LEAVES OBJECTS. 'CELEBRATE CCA's 50th BIRTHDAY WITH AN ADVENTURE INTO THE PAST - 1936-1986. 1986 is the CCA's fiftieth birthday. Your camp can take part in the celebration this summer! All across the country camps will participate by including one or all of the following activities in their programs: HISTORICAL JOURNEYS; RE-ENACTMENT OF EARLY CAMPING LIFESTYLES; CEREMONIES AND THEME EVENTS. Each participating camp will be recognized with A WALL CERTIFICATE and those camps pre-registering will receive CARDS FOR EACH OF THEIR CAMPERS.' Registration forms went through the provincial associations, so the ACQ held the Quebec list. TWO THINGS TO LOOK FOR: a KANAWANA WALL CERTIFICATE dated 1986 (dining-hall walls and photographs), and a camper's card from summer 1986. Ask Trent and the ACQ for the registration lists -- those would say directly whether Kanawana took part. Together with the May 1985 IYY 'historical roots' kit this makes TWO SUCCESSIVE SUMMERS in which every member camp in Canada was asked to research and perform its own history, both inside the 1980-1986 window for which no Kanawana season report survives. UPDATE 2026-09-05 (issue 158): THE PRE-FOUNDING MINUTES MAY EXIST. Adele Ebbs, Taylor Statten's daughter, describing the supper club of six private camp directors that preceded the CCA -- Mary S. Edgar (Glen Bernard), Mary G. Hamilton (Tanamakoon), Ferna Halliday (Oconto), Ernie Chapman (Kagawong), A. L. Cochrane (Temagami) and Statten, meeting four or five times a year in each other's homes in the early 1930s -- says: 'I was secretary, I FINALLY STARTED TO TAKE NOTES SOMETIME BEFORE I GOT MARRIED, AND THAT WAS 1935.' Minutes of the pre-founding meetings therefore exist from about 1934-35, kept by Ebbs, who was later Archives chairman for both the CCA and the OCA. ASK TRENT FOR THEM BY THAT DESCRIPTION -- they would settle the 1936/1938/c.1947 founding-date question outright. Also from the same interview: the early CCA presidential sequence is given as Taylor Statten, Dais Gass, Anne Vail, TED YARD, Irv Haladner, F. M. Van Wagner -- placing Ted Yard, the Camp Pine Crest director whose ceremony text this read recorded at issue 145, among the association's first presidents. ||| ADDED 2026-09-05 (issue 159, Canadian Camping Vol. 38 No. 2, Fall 1986). (1) *** THE STRONGEST NEW LEAD IN THIS READ: A NATIONAL YMCA COSTING SURVEY THAT SHOULD NAME KANAWANA. *** Shirley Yard, interviewed about her husband W. E. (Ted) Yard: 'There was a project of the Boys' Work Committee of the National Council YMCA. It is a survey of costs and factors in Canadian YMCA Camps. This is probably what he did his thesis on when he completed his Master's degree at George Williams College in 1958/59.' A national YMCA camp costing survey of 1958-59 is very unlikely to have omitted the YMCA of Montreal's own resident camp, and it would report Kanawana FROM OUTSIDE the Montreal association's files -- precisely what is missing for 1947-1967, since the Montreal annual reports of those years name no paid camp director and give Kanawana no separate accounting. WHERE TO LOOK: George Williams College thesis holdings (the college's records went to Aurora University, Illinois); the Kautz Family YMCA Archives at the University of Minnesota, which hold National Council material of this period; and the YMCA Canada national office records. Search terms: Yard, W. E. / Ted Yard; 'costs and factors'; Boys' Work Committee; George Williams College MS thesis 1958 or 1959. Written into wiki/history/postwar-gap.md as a lead, explicitly not as evidence that Kanawana appears in it. (2) The Ted Yard CAMP DIRECTOR'S CALENDAR, compiled 1959 at George Williams College and still in circulation in 1986 -- a month-by-month administrative calendar; useful as a period benchmark for what a camp director's year contained. (3) REPERTOIRE DE L'INVENTAIRE DES CAMPS D'EXPRESSION FRANCAISE (INCEF), second edition launched autumn 1986, data gathered by M. Jean-Luc Cote of the Conseil de la Vie francaise en Amerique, 59 rue d'Auteuil, Quebec G1R 4C2. Would map every French-language camp in Canada as of 1986. Ask the Conseil's successor and the ACQ. (4) *** ASK THE ACQ ABOUT THE SUMMER OF 1986 BEFORE ASKING WHAT IT HOLDS. *** Its 1986 report records that Employment and Immigration Canada funded a three-person team that spent that summer RECLASSIFYING ALL OF THE ACQ'S ARCHIVES AND CAMP DOSSIERS. The present arrangement of the ACQ's own records dates from that project; a request should be framed in its terms (camp dossiers, by camp) rather than in pre-1986 terms. The same report names the three accreditation consultants of 1986 -- Leo Venditti, Yves Legault, Louis Jean -- who between them visited 76 camps; Kanawana changed director inside FY1986 and by the ACQ's own stated rule should be among them. (5) 400 slides shot at Quebec camps in summer 1986 by Jean-Marc Amyot of the R.L.Q. audio-visual service for a bilingual slide show -- a dated photographic survey of Quebec camps that may include Kanawana; ask the ACQ and BAnQ. ||| ADDED 2026-09-05 (issue 160, Canadian Camping Vol. 38 No. 3, Winter 1987). (1) *** THE 50TH ANNIVERSARY OF QUEBEC CAMPING, 1988. *** Ken Willis, CCA/ACC Vice-President (Quebec Region): 'The organized camping movement in Quebec was born in 1938. TONY SHORGUN, who has been involved in camping during many of the intervening years, is already at work laying plans for the 50th Anniversary of this birth which, obviously, will be held next year.' If the event happened it produced a programme, press coverage or a commemorative publication assembled by a participant -- a history of Quebec camping in which Kanawana, a member camp throughout, would appear. Shorgun is a name new to this project: search obituaries, ACQ records, La Presse and the Gazette for 1988, and ask the ACQ directly. Note the run itself stops in 1988, so the magazine may not have covered it -- the last four issues should be watched for it. (2) BIG COVE YMCA CAMP now has three founding dates -- 1889 (encyclopaedic), 1890 (Jack Pearse, 1979), 1891 (Kelley Byrne, the camp's own director and president of the Nova Scotia association, 1987). Kanawana's second-oldest position is unaffected by all three, but if the wiki keeps asserting a date for Canada's oldest camp it should be sourced from a Nova Scotia primary record, not from any of these. Ask the Camping Association of Nova Scotia and the Halifax YMCA. (3) PROVINCIAL ASSOCIATION ARCHIVES. Bruno Morawetz, 1987: 'Some Provincial Associations have their own archives where they collect printed material about their member camps.' With the ACQ's summer-1986 archive reclassification (issue 159), that is two independent reasons to ask the QUEBEC association what it holds on Kanawana rather than only Trent. (4) Mary S. Edgar's memoir 'Turn of the Century for Suzanne Marie' remains the lead recorded earlier; the 1987 interview adds that her fonds came to Trent through John and Barb Gilchrist, who are the people to ask about anything Edgar kept from her Oolahwan years (1915-1919) -- the Quebec YWCA camp that visited Kanawana. ||| ADDED 2026-09-05 (issue 161, Canadian Camping Vol. 38 No. 4, Spring 1987). (1) A LETTER WENT TO THE QUEBEC ASSOCIATION IN FEBRUARY 1987 asking it to gather records AND to tape people. Bruno Morawetz: 'In February of this year a letter was sent to all Provincial Archives Chairmen, or to the Provincial President... I would urge your member camps to collect as much written material as possible and have it lodged in your own provincial archives... One of the ways of collecting archival material is to interview persons who are playing important roles in camping -- these too can be lodged and catalogued in an archival collection.' With the ACQ's summer-1986 archive reclassification (issue 159) and Morawetz's note that some provincial associations already held their own archives (issue 160), that is a THIRD prompt inside eighteen months for Quebec camping records to be assembled somewhere other than Trent. Ask the ACQ specifically whether it holds tapes or transcripts made after February 1987. (2) INCEF '87, the second edition of the repertoire des camps d'expression francaise hors Quebec, was PUBLISHED at the end of January 1987 with funding from the Conseil de la Vie francaise en Amerique and the Ministre des Affaires Intergouvernementales, copies held at the CCA office in Toronto. A dated, findable document. (3) EILEEN MAYOTTE was alive and donating to the CCA Patrons' Fund in 1987 -- the latest fixed point this project has for her, and a reason to look for an obituary from 1987 or later rather than earlier. She was QCA secretary in the 1940s and later president of the Saskatchewan association; a stub is warranted. (4) PAGE 7 OF THIS ISSUE ('Between the Covers', by Nancy Barker) produced no machine-readable text in the Internet Archive scan and has NOT been read. If a clean copy is ever obtained, that page is outstanding. ||| ADDED 2026-09-05 (issue 162, Canadian Camping Vol. 39 No. 1, Summer 1987). (1) A DATED TAPE IN THE CCA FONDS AT TRENT. Jocelyn Palm, writing Mary Northway's memorial: 'In 1981, I interviewed Dr. Northway in order that the tape could be added to the CCA Archives. I have just listened to that tape.' So a Palm-Northway interview tape existed in the Trent fonds and was playable in 1987. Northway 'engineered the collection and organization of the OCA and CCA Archives now at Trent University' -- she is the reason the collection this project depends on exists, and the tape is a specific, findable item. She died 26 February 1987. (2) THE OLDEST-CAMP QUESTION (see c_031): ask the YMCA-YWCA of Winnipeg and Manitoba provincial archives what the 1891 'Lake of the Woods Institute' actually was, and whether Camp Stephens's 1991 centenary produced a published history; ask the Camping Association of Nova Scotia and the Halifax YMCA for a primary record of Big Cove's first season. Kanawana's national ranking depends on both answers. (3) The CCA/ACC held its Board of Management and President's Council ANNUAL MEETING IN QUEBEC CITY, 1-3 May 1987, hosted by the ACQ, with visits to Camp Keno (Marist Fathers, chemin Saint-Louis) and Camp Oasis Notre-Dame (lac Simon, Portneuf). Pere Paul Belanger, a FORMER CCA VICE-PRESIDENT, received the council -- a Quebec name new to this project and worth researching. Minutes of that meeting would be in the Trent 'brown bag' accession for 1987. ||| ADDED 2026-09-05 (issue 163, Canadian Camping Vol. 39 No. 2, Fall 1987). (1) *** A DEMOGRAPHIC SURVEY OF QUEBEC CAMP CLIENTELE. *** ACQ president Henri Chalifoux, autumn 1987: a study 'to identify our summer camp clientele', funded by the ministere des Loisirs, de la Chasse et de la Peche (M.L.C.P.), renewing user research first done in 1982. If either the 1982 study or its 1987-88 renewal survives it would describe the population Kanawana drew from -- the only such source this read has encountered. Ask the ACQ and BAnQ; the M.L.C.P.'s successor ministry holds the funding records. (2) HENRI CHALIFOUX, ACQ president in 1987 and Quebec's national representative, is a name new to this project. So is the fact that FIVE consultants visited over 80 Quebec camps in summer 1987, ten of them applying for first-time ACQ membership. Kanawana was a member throughout; a 1987 visitation report should exist. (3) MATERIAL SENT TO THE MAGAZINE MAY NOT BE AT TRENT. The 'Jackpot!' notice states that the magazine forwarded donated memorabilia 'to the Canadian Camping Association Archives at Trent University OR to the appropriate provincial camping association archives in the camp's home province'. Third statement in three consecutive issues that provincial associations held their own archives. Quebec material from 1986-88 may be with the ACQ. (4) EILEEN MAYOTTE was on the Commission des camps d'expression francaise for 1987-88 (as Saskatchewan's member) AND donated to the Patrons' Fund that year -- two independent fixed points in 1987 for the QCA's 1940s secretary. KEN WILLIS stayed on as the committee's Quebec member after retiring as vice-president. (5) INCEF 1988 was planned, to carry a review ('bilan') of the three French-language camp inventories made since 1985 -- the single most useful of the INCEF documents if it was published, and the run stops in 1988. (6) PARC completed a NATIONAL SURVEY of physical activity programmes at Canadian camps in 1987 with a high response rate; the summary was promised for the next issue, which is the last one the magazine published. Watch issue 164. ||| ADDED 2026-09-05 (issue 164, Canadian Camping Vol. 39 No. 3, Winter 1988 -- THE LAST ISSUE; the word-for-word read of all 164 issues is now complete). (1) *** A. ROSS SEAMAN DIED 23 OCTOBER 1987. *** Exact date, from the memorial fund notice. This narrows an obituary search to the last week of October and the first weeks of November 1987 -- The Review (Vankleek Hill), the Montreal Gazette, and Concordia's own newsletters. The A. Ross Seaman Leadership Development Fund was founded by family, friends and colleagues meeting in EARLY NOVEMBER 1987, with a minimum goal of $25,000, interest only, administered by Universite Concordia, Bureau des finances AD 130. CONCORDIA'S OWN FINANCE AND ADVANCEMENT RECORDS for that fund are a documented, named, findable file about a Kanawana director -- ask for the fund's establishing file and its founding donor list, which will name the family, friends and colleagues who met in November 1987. (2) THE ACQ'S FOIRE DES CAMPS at the COMPLEXE DESJARDINS, MONTREAL, early 1988, with the ACQ as maitre d'oeuvre. A public camp fair in downtown Montreal that Kanawana as a member camp had every reason to attend; it would have produced press coverage (La Presse, Le Devoir, the Gazette, January-March 1988) and a printed programme listing exhibitors. (3) MADELENE ALLEN, director of Camp Ouareau, joined the ACQ's Conseil d'administration at the start of 1988, replacing Ken Willis.
