priorities.description: ESTABLISH WHETHER KANAWANA RAN AN INTERCULTURAL CAMPING PROJECT IN 1965. May Brown's president's report, Canadian Camping Vol. 18 No. 1 (December 1965), records "Intercultural or Intergroup Camping projects" run by "a number of our member camps" over the summer of 1965, with the CCA executive gathering information and exploring an Evaluation and Training Seminar. Kanawana was a member camp, and the movement is the same one Hedley Dimock reported on from Goldeye Lake, Alberta in April 1965 -- Dimock being the man who had run counsellor research at Kanawana five years earlier and who by then chaired the Applied Social Science Division at Sir George Williams. Check the YMCA of Montreal annual reports for 1965 and 1966 and the CCA's own files for the list of participating camps.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 65-68, converted to KB facts

priorities.description:
FIND THE QCA'S 1965 INSPECTION REPORT ON KANAWANA. Canadian Camping Vol. 18 No. 3 (April 1966), "From the Provinces": "Quebec's concern for standards resulted in their securing the services of Mr. Murray McFarlane who visited twenty-seven camps during the summer months, and completed an exhaustive report on each camp. The camps were charged $25.00 for the visit, said visit to be made one every three years. A detailed report was submitted to the Standards Committee, and letters of accreditation were then forwarded to twenty-five camps which passed. Notices went to the two who did not meet the standards." That is the Quebec Camping Association's first documented accreditation round: a paid inspector, twenty-seven camps, an individual written report on each, a three-year cycle. Kanawana was a QCA member camp of exactly this size and type, so an exhaustive written 1965 report on the camp -- site, sanitation, waterfront, programme, staff -- was very probably produced and filed. This is the most specific and most promising archival lead the whole word-for-word read has produced for this wiki's own subject. WHERE TO LOOK: the Association des camps du Quebec's own records; the CCA/ACC fonds at Trent; the YMCA of Montreal fonds at Concordia for the camp's own copy and for the $25 payment in the accounts. NAME CAUTION: the inspector is very likely the P. M. McFarlane who wrote the Montreal MacKay Centre camp article in April 1965 -- a former camp director, therefore qualified to inspect -- but the given names differ in the two notices; record both and do not merge without a third source.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 100): QUEBEC ACCREDITATION IS OLDER THAN 1965. The tribute read when the QCA English Section made Mrs. Alta R. Kahn its first Honorary President on 23 May 1973 records that she was Co-Chairman of the QCA Standards Committee in 1959-60, 'when inspection of camps and accreditation were in the pioneer stage.' So the machinery predates the 1965 McFarlane round by five or six years, and the search window for a written Kanawana accreditation report opens correspondingly earlier. The same tribute dates the association's Provincial Charter to 1961 -- a corporate record Quebec's register of enterprises should hold, and the most concrete handle yet on where the association's own papers went.

FURTHER AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 103): QUEBEC RE-ACCREDITED EVERY CAMP ANNUALLY. John Hasell, chairman of the CCA National Standards Committee, in the January 1975 Directory Issue: other provinces required 'a visit every two or three years, but Quebec has developed its programme to the point where every camp is re-accredited annually' -- printed in both languages. So what is missing is not one report but a SERIES: an annual, itemised, externally written assessment of Kanawana's administration, personnel practices, site, programme, health and safety, running from about 1960 (Kahn's 'pioneer stage', 1959-60) to whenever the camp's accreditation lapsed. Two named handles for the request: the QCA English Section had an ARCHIVES chairman in 1975, Mr. Joseph A. Hood, so the Section was actively keeping records; and its Executive Secretary, Miss Frances M. Kelly, ran a STAFF PLACEMENT BUREAU from 2233 Belgrave Avenue, which would have generated its own record of who worked at which Quebec camp. Ask for both by name.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 69-71, converted to KB facts

priorities.description:
SPAWN A STUB FOR DAIS L. GASS, and one for Camp Memphremagog. Gass appears on every masthead in this read as a Montreal past president of the Canadian Camping Association with nothing else attached. Five tributes printed in Vol. 18 No. 4 (June 1966), after her death on 14 February 1966, give her a life: born in Nova Scotia, a graduate of Mount Allison University; to Montreal as a teacher at Trafalgar Girls' School; later personnel worker for the T. Eaton Company; a CGIT leader and YWCA camp volunteer; founder of Camp Memphremagog for Girls in the Eastern Townships in 1946, where campers called her "Kolali", "Friend"; second President of the CCA, 1946-49, succeeding Taylor Statten; chair of the meetings in Montreal, Toronto and Kingston that produced "the first official charter of the Canadian Camping Association"; and Past-President of the Quebec Camping Association. Camp Memphremagog was sold to the United Church in 1959 and run thereafter as a boys' camp. She is one of very few women among the movement's founders and a Montreal figure this project has been listing without knowing anything about. NOTE A DISCREPANCY TO CARRY, NOT RESOLVE: Mary Edgar's tribute says "During her twenty-three years as Director," which does not square with 1946-59 and may count her whole camping career.

AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 92): DAIS L. GASS IS NOW IDENTIFIED WELL ENOUGH TO WRITE. Charles Plewman's founding history of the magazine (Vol. 24 No. 1, Fall 1971) names "Miss Dais L. Gass, president of the C.C.A. in 1946" as the author of Canadian Camping's first editorial, and quotes it in full: "Now it starts in its humble way -- may it grow like the acorn and the oak, but most of all may it prove a tie between all of us in Canada... May Canadian Camping weave a bond of understanding, of mutual helpfulness and good will from sea to sea, and from the rivers to the end of the earth." With W. E. Yard's 1966 tribute, which credits her with chairing the Montreal, Toronto and Kingston meetings that produced the CCA's first official charter, she is now a Montreal woman who presided over the national association at its formation and wrote the first words of its magazine, and still has no KB fact of her own beyond this read. That is enough for a stub. Search: Montreal YWCA records, Camp Memphremagog, McGill and Sir George Williams alumni records, and Gazette obituaries.

FURTHER AMENDMENT (extraction pass, issue 94): A BOUND ON HER DEATH. The CCA past-presidents list in Vol. 24 No. 3 (Spring 1972) marks Taylor Statten of Toronto and Dais L. Gass of Montreal with asterisks as deceased, while Anne I. Vail, F. M. Van Wagner and Kenneth H. Murray, also Montreal, carry none. So Gass died before Spring 1972 -- the first bound this read has produced -- and the three unasterisked Montreal past presidents were living in 1972. That narrows an obituary search considerably.

priorities.description: SEARCH THE SAINT-SAUVEUR AND MONTREAL PRESS OF SUMMER 1967 FOR KANAWANA'S CENTENARY JOURNEY DEPARTURE. John Latimer, chairman of the CCA's Centenary Journey Committee, wrote in Vol. 18 No. 4 (June 1966) that "the administration in Ottawa is not convinced that we deserve their support" and asked every director to contact local radio, TV and newspaper editors when a trip left camp. That is a direct instruction to generate local press coverage of departing trips, which makes the local papers a much better bet for a Kanawana notice than this project has assumed. The same article describes the NATIONAL CENTENARY CAMPFIRE -- "hundreds and hundreds of Campfires, lit at exactly the same time, on the same day in the summer of 1967 ... with the same opening and closing used by everyone who participates," in every camp in Canada and on every canoe trip. voyageur-canoe-pageant.md records that a National Campfire was held on 9 August 1967; this is the plan behind it, and it means Kanawana almost certainly lit one, from a prescribed text that is itself a specific thing to look for. Also findable: the minutes of the March 1966 Toronto conference of all ten provincial Centenary chairmen, at which "the final and official routes were mapped ... safety standards were developed ... Rendezvous Points were established" -- which would fix Kanawana's leg exactly.

priorities.description: ANSWER OPEN QUESTION 8 IN camp-oolahwan.md. That article records as a confirmed dead end -- "Confirmed dead end across Trent, McCord, and LAC catalog descriptions -- no successor-director name found online" -- the question of who directed Camp Oolahwan after Mary Edgar left in 1919. Faye Ecclestone's profile of the Canadian Camping Association's national president, Canadian Camping Vol. 19 No. 1 (December 1966), supplies a name: "she went east to Montreal where she joined the staff of the Y.W.C.A. in that city. Her responsibilities included directing Camp Oolawahn and she also took the opportunity of completing her B.Sc. in Physical Education at McGill University." That is Mrs. Lorne E. (May) Brown, CCA president 1964-67 and later a Vancouver Parks Board figure. Internal dating from the same profile -- UBC teaching after graduation, marriage, children born about 1950 and 1955, an M.P.E. in 1961, Camp Deka founded about 1961 -- puts the Oolahwan directorship in the 1940s, most plausibly the later 1940s. WRITE IT UP WITH THE CAVEAT: the exact years still need a second source, and the LAC series that article already flags, "Camp Oolahwan committee minutes, reports and training programmes, 1916-1974," should settle them. Note also that Camp Deka, Brown's own camp, is already recorded in voyageur-canoe-pageant.md as a Centenary Journey participant -- so the national president's camp paddled the journey Kanawana paddled.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 72-74, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: FIND THE MARY S. EDGAR POEM WRITTEN FOR THE NATIONAL CENTENARY CAMPFIRE. The OCA's "OCAsional News" of December 1966, quoted in Canadian Camping Vol. 19 No. 2 (February 1967): "The biggest of these activities is the National Campfire to be held Wednesday, August 9, 1967. On this night each camp will be provided with ideas for suitable programmes, centering around the Voyageur theme. It is hoped that a common opening and closing can be written including a poem for the occasion by Miss Mary Edgar. At the pre-set time every camp across the country will light its campfire!... There may even be a programme on a coast to coast radio network to coincide with the lighting of the campfires." Edgar founded and first edited this magazine and wrote "God Who Touchest Earth With Beauty." A poem written for a single simultaneous national campfire is a findable text, and if Kanawana lit a fire that night its campers heard it. WHERE TO LOOK: Edgar's collections A Christmas Wreath of Verse (1965) and Once There Was a Camper (1970); her fonds at Trent and Queen's; the OCA archive founded in 1966 under Margaret Govan; and the prepared programme packet camps were sent, which is itself a distributable document to hunt for. ALSO FIND: the 1967 Canadian Camping Conference "Digest," sold at three dollars, which Bruno Morawetz calls "that encyclopedia of camping" -- the fullest single record of Canadian camping thinking in the Centennial year.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 72-74, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: PATCH THE NATIONAL CENTENARY CAMPFIRE INTO centennial-1967.md, AND UPDATE a-ross-seaman.md. Canadian Camping Vol. 19 No. 4 (June 1967) prints the complete National Campfire ceremony distributed to every camp in Canada: the timing ("at varying times from 7 p.m. in the Yukon to 12:30 a.m. in Newfoundland," so about 11 p.m. EDT in Quebec on Wednesday 9 August 1967, with a warning to allow for Daylight time); the Fire-lighter call; the oration; the "Indian prayer" from the Centennial Anthology of Prayer; the thirteen-song list, including "Land of the Silver Birch"; the closing torch-light circle and Taps; and the suggestion of a birthday cake baked in a reflector oven. And it prints Mary S. Edgar's commissioned text, "Canada's Our Country," words by Edgar to the hymn tune Hermas, performed by a Toronto boys' choir at the annual meeting of 1 March 1967. NOTE WHAT THIS DEMONSTRATES: the A. Ross Seaman profile in the SAME issue has already been mined -- a-ross-seaman.md quotes it as its footnote 9 -- while the campfire script beside it appears nowhere in the wiki or the KB. Somebody went to this document looking for Seaman, found him, and stopped. Separately, that article should gain from this stretch of the run: Seaman as CCA vice-president for Quebec from December 1966; as president of the QCA English Section to September 1967, stepping down to a vice-presidency at the board elected at Expo on 23 September 1967; and as the resource person the Maritimes brought in to teach "Methods of Measurement in Camping" and "Methods of Evaluation" at the first Atlantic Provinces seminar, Moncton, 17-19 November 1967. [DONE 2026-09-05. Part (a), the National Campfire ceremony, was already written into history/centennial-1967.md by the read pass -- section 'The National Campfire, 9 August 1967', with the Fire-lighter call, the timing across time zones, Mary Edgar's 'Canada's Our Country' to the tune Hermas, and footnote 22 noting explicitly that an earlier pass took the Seaman profile from this same issue and left the ceremony untouched. Part (b) is done here: a-ross-seaman.md now dates his CCA vice-presidency for Quebec to December 1966 - spring 1968 and his QCA presidency to roughly 1966 - 23 September 1967, when the Provincial Board elected at Expo moved him to a vice-presidency; and records the Moncton seminar of 17-19 November 1967 where he taught 'Methods of Measurement in Camping' and 'Methods of Evaluation'. The last of those bears on how Kanawana's own staff-assessment paperwork of the period should be read.]
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 75-77, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR WALLACE FORGIE. He is now one of the most connected figures in the whole word-for-word read, and his signed obituary in Canadian Camping Vol. 20 No. 2 (Winter 1968), by J. H. Ebbs, M.D. -- his nephew by marriage -- supplies the frame: born 1883, died 1 December 1967; "known as 'Commodore' by the many young leaders who came under his influence in Canada from 1908 until 1927"; five years overseas with the YMCA in the First World War; boys' work in Western Canada "during which he conducted many canoe trips into the north-west"; "an associate of the late Dr. Hedley Dimock who was succeeded by Professor Charles E. Hendry"; and Camp Tonakela near Madras, built 1935, followed by "thirty-two years of voluntary service," where the Indian children called him "Tah-Tah" and the head of the Child Health Institute of Madras said he "will be remembered in this part of the world as an Albert Schweitzer." To that the read adds: he photographed C. F. Plewman at the Lake Couchiching YMCA camp in 1903; he built the foundations of Camp On-Da-Da-Waks and moved the Ottawa camp to Golden Lake in 1908; he held the Alberta YMCA boys'-work post that Hendry took over when he left in 1927; he worked in South India and Ceylon from 1927 to 1936; and he was Adele Statten Ebbs's uncle, taking her on her first canoe trip through Temagami at ten -- which makes him kin to Taylor Statten, either Ethel Statten's brother or the husband of Statten's sister Bolina. Settling which is a specific genealogical question worth answering, and taylor-statten.md should say so once it is.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 75-77, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: RECOVER THE QUEBEC CAMP ACCREDITATION STANDARDS THROUGH THEIR FRENCH TRANSLATION. Lionel Perras, president of l'Association des camps du Quebec, writing in Canadian Camping Vol. 22 No. 3 (April 1970): "L'Association fournit aux camps avec le texte des normes actuelles dernierement traduites de la QCA" -- the ACQ's standards are a recent translation of the Quebec Camping Association's. So if the English QCA text Kanawana was measured against is lost, the French version recovers its content. Perras also points directly at where to look: accreditation "fut l'une des premieres preoccupations des fondateurs de l'ACQ en 1958... il suffit de relire les proces-verbaux des assemblees" -- the ACQ's own minutes from 1958 onward. His article sets out the eleven characteristics assessed and the six-heading self-critique in full, so even without the standards text the shape of a camp's accreditation file is now known: administration (including "Y a-t-il un Coutumier du camp?", a book of the camp's own customs, required by the accreditation process); programme; resources; la vie des campeurs; finances; and hygiene, health and safety. He refers besides to "des camps visites au cours de l'ete 1966" -- a second Quebec visiting round, the year after Murray McFarlane's twenty-seven-camp round of 1965 (p_339). Chase both rounds together. NOTE ALSO the mandatory national standards implemented in 1970 under Ron Johnstone as National Chairman of Standards, "Over 20 items are mandatory for a Camp to be an accredited member" -- which is the regime Kanawana operated under from that year.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 84-86, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: READ THE FRENCH-LANGUAGE CONTENT OF CANADIAN CAMPING FROM APRIL 1970. The magazine went bilingual with Vol. 22 No. 3 (April 1970): cover, masthead, the Prime Minister's editorial and Elsie Palter's article all in both languages, and Lionel Perras contributing a full-length article IN FRENCH ONLY. That is a fact about the source as much as about the movement: from April 1970 the run carries French-language material that an English-only search would never surface, and the word-for-word read has been catching it only because it is a word-for-word read. When the remaining issues are extracted, the French content needs the same attention as the English -- and any earlier pass over this corpus that used English keyword search should be assumed to have missed it entirely. The provincial offices list from that issue gives two addresses to chase separately: Quebec Camping Association, 2233 Belgrave Ave., Montreal 261, and L'Association des camps de Quebec, 952 Cherrier Ave., Montreal.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 84-86, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: QUERY TRENT UNIVERSITY ARCHIVES FOR THE ONTARIO CAMPING ASSOCIATION FONDS -- AND SPECIFICALLY FOR ITS TAPED INTERVIEWS. Mary Northway's account in Canadian Camping, November 1970, dates the deposit exactly: 22 October 1970, past president John Latimer handing the archives to Dr. T. H. B. Symons at Trent, six years' work by a committee chaired successively by Adele Ebbs, Margaret Govan and Northway herself, catalogued at the OCA office by Mrs. Shirley Hall. Contents as she lists them: early brochures, photographs, programmes and schedules, films, financial accounts, diaries, AND TAPED INTERVIEWS OF PROMINENT CAMP PERSONALITIES. The collecting policy was 'everything. Let the archivist decide what is not important' -- so the fonds should contain national and inter-provincial material, not only Ontario. Three specific asks: (a) the taped interviews, and whether any interviewee had Quebec or YMCA connections; (b) the minute David Palter quotes from the Legislative Committee meeting of 7 March 1957, which should be in these papers; (c) whether the fonds includes CCA material from the years the national office was at 102 Eglinton Ave. East inside the OCA office (from 1971). A duplicate file was kept at the camping office; the originals went to Trent.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 87-89, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: FIND MARY S. EDGAR'S 'ONCE THERE WAS A CAMPER' (G. R. Welch, Toronto, 1970) AND RECORD 'HYMN FOR THE SPACE-AGE'. Canadian Camping, November 1970, announces the book as 'a little book of 23 delightful rhymes on kids at camp' with the author's own line drawings, and prints in the same issue Edgar's 'Hymn for the Space-Age' (Tune: Forest Green), an explicitly environmental hymn by the CCA's honorary president -- the third Edgar hymn this read has found, after 'Canada's Our Country' (June 1967) and 'This Fair Land, Our Canada' (1969). Search: Library and Archives Canada, Toronto Public Library, University of Toronto, Trent (the OCA fonds), AbeBooks and Internet Archive. The hymn text belongs in environmental-and-ecological-history and alongside the Edgar material in centennial-1967.md.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 87-89, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: DID KANAWANA SEND A DELEGATE TO THE CCA NATIONAL CONFERENCE ON CAMPING STANDARDS AND RESEARCH, HALIFAX, 22-23 FEBRUARY 1971? The conference was one delegate per member camp, with the CCA board meeting 20-21 February and the annual meeting on the evening of the 21st; delegates were asked to propose topics under standards and accreditation, health and safety, leadership development, and pollution and conservation. A delegate list, if it was printed in a later issue of Canadian Camping, would place a named Kanawana staff member at a national meeting on a precise date. Check the Spring and Summer 1971 issues in the cached run when the read reaches them, and the YMCA of Montreal's own 1971 records.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 87-89, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: READ KANAWANA'S SONG RECORD AGAINST JACK PEARSE'S 'SONG LEADING' (Canadian Camping, June 1970) -- the p_048 comparator the read was looking for. Pearse, director of Camp Tawingo, sets out the period's own five-category taxonomy (novelty numbers, action songs, rounds, spirituals and folk songs, quiet songs) with a named repertoire under each, plus the rule that all sing-songs end quietly and the advice that leaders should make up songs for their own groups. This does three things for the Kanawana song question: it dates the common stock (so a Kanawana song found in Pearse's lists is movement-wide, not camp-specific); it supplies the vocabulary the period actually used for its own singing; and it establishes that camp-specific songs were an advised practice, not an accident. Any traditions article on Kanawana singing should distinguish the common stock from the camp's own on this basis, and say which it is doing. | DONE 2026-09-05. Pearse's five categories are now a table in camp-songs-cheers.md with his named repertoire under each, his eight-step method for teaching a round, and the rule he prints in capitals: ALL SING SONGS SHOULD END WITH QUIET SINGING (f_4869). THE COMPARISON THE PRIORITY WANTED, and it cuts both ways as it should. TWO KANAWANA SONGS ARE IN HIS LISTS: Kum Bah Yah, which he classes under spirituals and folk songs, and 'My Old Kentucky Home' -- sung solo by a twelve-year-old in the 1938 broadcast -- which is a Stephen Foster song, the first entry in his quiet category. Neither is Kanawana property; both are the movement's common stock, and the article says so, so no later pass reads either as evidence of anything local. AND THE CAMP'S OWN SONGS ARE WHAT THE MOVEMENT TOLD LEADERS TO MAKE: 'On My Way to Kanawana', the Marching Song, 'Dear Old Kanawana' to the Battle Hymn, the Alabama Jubilee adaptation -- all fall under Pearse's novelty category, whose instruction is not a description but an order, 'Find some novelty numbers. Invent some.' Camp-specific songs were ADVISED PRACTICE, taught as technique in the association's own magazine. That is better founded than either 'Kanawana's songs are unusual' or 'Kanawana's songs are borrowed' (f_4870). Pearse's closing rule also matches Kay McClelland's 1956 campfire structure already held here (f_2725). camp-songs-cheers.md 23 -> 24 sources.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 87-89, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: REVISE THE CHOPSY LINE OF ENQUIRY (p_045) IN LIGHT OF DAVID HARTRY'S 'SNARK HUNTING' (Canadian Camping, Winter 1971). Hartry, then CCA president, documents his own camp's legend from the inside: invented for the first official hunt in 1968 at the Anglican Youth Camp near Halifax, staged by setting campers' watches ahead, the creature built by campers who had been let in on the secret the year before, given a spurious documentary pedigree by a book found in the camp library, and within three years expected annually and already being elaborated in campers' own vocabulary. It tells us nothing about Chopsy. It tells us what kind of evidence a legend like Chopsy leaves: the staging is remembered, the invention is not, and apparent corroboration may be part of the hoax. The DRAFT_ORAL_HISTORY_INSTRUMENT should therefore ask about staging, about who was let in on it and when, and about whether anyone was ever shown 'proof' -- not only about the story as told.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 87-89, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: SPAWN STUBS FOR THE THREE FOUNDERS' NAMES NOW DOCUMENTED FROM CANADIAN CAMPING: Charles Plewman (owner-director of Kilcoo Camp, past president of the OCA, camping from 1909, made an Honorary Member at the Society of Camp Directors' Founders' Meeting, wrote Ethel Statten's obituary); W. Bertram Danson (Camp Winnebagoe, present at the 7 March 1957 OCA Legislative Committee meeting, author of the June 1970 'Do's and Don'ts for Counsellors' with its ban on physical punishment); and David Palter, B.Sc., P.Eng., camp consultant, appointed OCA Standards Committee chairman 29 April 1957 and the man who started Canadian camp accreditation. NOTE FOR THE STUB ON PALTER: he is not David Paltiel, the Kanawana name on the Knights of Kanawana roll, the 1975 board and the 1976 staff list. Different names, no evidence of any link; the stub must say so.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 87-89, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: CHECK BRITISH COLUMBIA'S SUMMER CAMP LICENSING AGAINST GERTRUDE 'DINTY' MOORE'S STANDARDS. Her obituary in Canadian Camping, November 1970, states that she founded the BC Camping Association in 1939, was its first president, and that during her ten years in executive office the association drew up standards for camping in the province with the provincial government, 'Later this research and study was used as a basis for Government licensing of summer camps in B.C.' If that holds, British Columbia licensed camps on standards a camp director wrote -- the outcome David Palter was still arguing for in Ontario in 1969, achieved a generation earlier. A checkable claim: search BC statutes and regulations on summer camps, the BC Camping Association's own history, and Moorecroft (the United Church site near Nanoose Bay she sold on retirement). Bears on how to read Quebec's own accreditation arrangements, which never became licensing.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 87-89, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: FIND THE PAPERS OF THE QUEBEC ASSOCIATION'S 1971 SEMINAR ON STAFF POLICY AND CAMP FINANCING. Huguette Dagenais reports in Canadian Camping, Summer 1971, that the merged A.C.Q.-Q.C.A. held a seminar for camp directors and their principal colleagues attended by 115 people, on 'politiques de personnel et des questions de financement dans les camps,' run bilingually without simultaneous translation with bilingual animateurs linking the two language groups. A weekend gathering of 115 Quebec camp directors on staff policy and camp financing in 1971 is exactly the forum a Kanawana director would have attended, and its working papers -- if they survive with the association's records -- bear directly on the p_307 staff-assessment thread and on how Quebec camps were financed in the period. Chase: the successor body to the ACQ-QCA and its archives, the Haut-Commissariat a la Jeunesse, aux Loisirs et aux Sports fonds at BAnQ (the association's $30,000 provincial grant means it reported to a ministry), and the association's own newsletter. Dagenais also records that thirteen people represented Quebec at the CCA congress in Halifax that year.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 90-91, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: TRACE YVES BEAUREGARD, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR OF THE MERGED QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION UNTIL 1 FEBRUARY 1971. Dagenais's 'Nouvelles du Quebec' (Spring 1971) records his departure on that date and gives him the title directeur-executif of the A.C.Q.-Q.C.A. -- so the merged Quebec association had a paid professional staff, and this is the first named holder of the post the read has found. A paid executive director keeps files: correspondence, membership records, accreditation reports. Finding him, or his successor, is the most direct route to the written accreditation record the p_339 thread is looking for. Search: Quebec recreation and youth-service directories of the period, BAnQ, Le Devoir and La Presse for the association's announcements, and LinkedIn or obituary sources for a man in a professional post in Montreal in the late 1960s.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 90-91, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: RECORD THE CCA'S 1971 REGIONAL RESTRUCTURING IN canadian-camping-movement.md, AND THE QUEBEC SUCCESSION WITH IT. Two things settle in 1971 that this read has been tracking through address changes since issue 80. (a) John Latimer's first president's letter (Summer 1971): 'since the Association was founded, the Executive moved from province to province every two years. Now there are five Vice-Presidents on the Executive of C.C.A. who represent various regions' -- Tom Creighton (Atlantic), Bob Lazanik (Quebec), Jack Pearse (Ontario), Eileen Mayotte (Prairie), Tanya Krisman (BC) -- ending the rotating provincial executive that had moved the national office Winnipeg to Halifax to Toronto. (b) David Hartry's 'C.C.A. -- New National Office' of 14 December 1970 gives the reason the federally funded Ottawa office closed after less than two years: project grants remained available but administrative grants did not, so the CCA moved into the OCA's office at $45 a month and operated from its own income. On the Quebec side, Perras hands the merged association's presidency to Robert Lazanik in 1971 and receives its insignia; the two-section structure with one president over it, printed at issue 89, holds.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 90-91, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: CHECK KANAWANA'S OWN RECORD AGAINST THE 1971 QUEBEC BUS-TRANSPORT PROCEDURE AND FIRE-SAFETY STANDARD. Two operations documents in the Summer 1971 issue set out what a well-run Quebec camp was expected to do, and both leave paper. Huguette Dagenais's 'Le camp de jour et son transport' requires tendering four months before opening, commercial permits and an insurance policy verified per vehicle by serial number, a monitor on every bus, and written camp rules for drivers. Deputy Chief Bryan Mitchell's 'Fire-Safe Camping' sets out fire permits from the Department of Lands and Forests, flammable-liquid storage, extinguisher placement with staff instructed in their use, and annual servicing of cooking, refrigeration and heating equipment by a qualified serviceman. If the YMCA of Montreal kept insurance schedules, bus contracts, or fire-inspection certificates for Kanawana, they would answer to these. Worth an explicit ask of the YMCA of Montreal's records alongside the accreditation request in p_339.

priorities.description: WRITE THE CANADIAN CAMPING SECTION OF meta/sources-index.md. The 164-issue run is the largest single body of source material this project holds and meta/sources-index.md still has no section on it at all. Charles Plewman's 'The Canadian Camping Magazine and How We Came By It' (Vol. 24 No. 1, Fall 1971) is the founding document and should anchor the section: the OCA formed 1933; Plewman drafted into its presidency autumn 1944; the T. Eaton Company financing the first edition; Mary Edgar as first editor; the Ontario Bulletin closed out in 1947 in favour of a mimeographed quarterly called Canadian Camping; and 'The first real Canadian Camping magazine was published in February of 1949 when for the first time it appeared in print' -- which is exactly where this project's cached run begins, so the run is complete from the first printed issue and the 1947-48 mimeographed bulletin is a separate body of material the project does not hold. Fred Haiblen of Toronto assumed the financial responsibility for going to print; Edgar edited five more years and was succeeded by Mrs. G. W. Flynn. THE SECTION'S FIRST STATEMENT MUST BE THE 1988 FUNDING CUT-OFF as the explanation of the run's end date. Other anchor facts already extracted: Jay Haddad's editorship mid-1981 to Winter 1986; the magazine passing to a Camp Tawingo group from Spring 1986; the 1967 publisher change to Town Talk Publications under Eanswythe Flynn; the December 1969 change to Broydon Printers and Groff's 'From mimeograph to letterpress to offset'; the April 1970 turn to bilingual publication (and with it the French-only content an English keyword search never surfaces -- see p_347); subscription rates ($3/year and $8/three in 1970, a $2 staff rate from 1971, $1.00 a single copy from Winter 1972, $8/$2 to 1987 and $10/$3 from 1987; ISSN 0834325); and the Fall 1971 statement that 'CANADIAN CAMPING is a 100% Canadian magazine and is not subsidized in any way. It is supported solely by advertisements.' [DONE 2026-09-05: written as the '*Canadian Camping* Magazine, February 1949 - Winter 1988' section of meta/sources-index.md. Leads with the 1988 Fitness Canada cut-off as the explanation of the run's end date; carries Plewman's founding history, the production/format/price table, the two warnings about the French text, the statement of what the run does and does not contain about Kanawana, and the register of known scan defects. The Edgar-vs-Plewman 'founder' discrepancy is recorded there unresolved.]

priorities.description: FIND OUT WHAT HAPPENED AT THE CHATEAU LAURIER IN 1946. Charles Plewman, first-hand, in Fall 1971: 'Before very long, I think it was in 1946, the Canadian Camping Association was formed at a meeting held in the Chateau Laurier in Ottawa' -- nearly all members representatives of the Ontario and Quebec associations, no other province then having one, and the body having 'no corporate existence' at that point. That is a second independent first-hand source for a 1946 event, against this project's documented 1936 founding at the Central YMCA, Toronto, and it corroborates the Camp Stephens claim that Nelson McEwen founded the CCA in 1946 (see c_035). The question is now concrete and checkable. Search: the CCA's own minutes, which by Mary Northway's account should be in the OCA archives deposited at Trent in October 1970 (p_348); Chateau Laurier function records; Ottawa press for 1946; and the incorporation file behind the 1949 charter, which Dais L. Gass chaired the meetings for.

priorities.description: CHECK WHETHER KANAWANA APPEARS AT THE CCA'S MONTREAL MEETINGS OF APRIL 1972. John Latimer's Winter 1972 newsletter gives the dates and the venue: the CCA Board meeting at the Queen Elizabeth Hotel, Montreal, 19-20 April 1972, the Annual Meeting the night of 20 April, and the QCA-ACQ Conference 20-22 April at the same hotel, with a separate Quebec Camping Association annual meeting on 24 May. A national camping conference held in Montreal, hosted by the Quebec association Kanawana belonged to, is the single most likely occasion in the whole run for the camp to appear by name -- as a host, a tour stop, a delegate, or an exhibitor. Read the Spring and Summer 1972 issues of the run for the conference report with this specifically in mind, and search Montreal press for 19-24 April 1972.

priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR THE SOCIETY OF CAMP DIRECTORS. Two accounts in the run now give it a full institutional history: J. Harry Ebbs's founding address (1969) and Clifford Labbett's 'The Society of Camp Directors' (Fall 1971). Ebbs's questionnaire to OCA members in 1968 was the seed; the founding banquet was at the Rosedale Golf Club, Toronto, in May 1969 (12 May per Labbett, 21 May per Ebbs -- see c_037), fifty-seven members attending; the purpose was 'to establish and maintain professional practices in the directing of childrens' camps and to ensure qualified directorship in such camps'; a board of five on three-year terms; three membership classes with Honorary Fellows Mary Edgar, Ferna Halliday, Mary Hamilton, Charles Plewman and Mrs. Taylor Statten elected at the inaugural dinner; meetings on the second Thursday of November and April; a $500 undergraduate research fund; and a joint proposal with the OCA for stricter licensing of children's camps with the OCA as governing body. The Society matters to this project because so many of the papers this read has surfaced were delivered to it, and because its licensing campaign is the professionalisation argument Quebec never resolved the same way.

priorities.description: REWRITE THE ORIGIN SECTION OF wiki/site/indigenous-names-and-land.md USING MARY EDGAR'S 1971 TESTIMONY. Her talk 'Our Indebtedness to Our Indian Friends,' given in the Glen Bernard chapel on 15 August 1971 and reprinted in Canadian Camping Vol. 24 No. 4 (Summer 1972), is the clearest contemporaneous statement the project holds of how 'Indian programming' reached Canadian camps, and it runs through Montreal. She names the channel in her own words: Pauline Johnson performing at Sundridge about 1899 and staying in the Edgar family home; the 1900 rescue on Lake Nipissing by two men from the Dokis Reserve, which she frames as a debt; and the YWCA training course in New York in 1914-15, where Ruby M. Jolliffe, Superintendent of State Camps for New York and New Jersey, introduced her to a storyteller Jolliffe 'often engaged... for Council Ring programs.' American state-camp practice, via the YWCA national training school, into a Canadian camp director's programme -- arriving at the Montreal YWCA's own Laurentian camp before Glen Bernard. Kanawana's totem pole (1927), Council Ring and 'Council of Tribes' belong to the same period and the same movement. Set beside it the Fall 1972 issue, which prints within two pages both a genuine transmission of Algonquin craft knowledge from William Commanda and a missionary pastiche presented as an Indigenous psalm, without appearing to notice the difference. Edgar's own language -- debt, shame, 'the white race will learn to appreciate' -- is recorded as written and dated, not adopted. [DONE 2026-09-05. The Edgar 1971 half was already written in by the read pass -- the 'Where the practice came from, in a founder's own words' passage, with Pauline Johnson at Sundridge c.1899, the 1900 Dokis Reserve rescue framed as a debt, and Ruby M. Jolliffe's New York state-camp storyteller in 1914-15, plus the Gilchrist and Northway material added later. The outstanding piece was the Fall 1972 juxtaposition, which was in the KB as f_3666/f_3667 and appeared nowhere in the wiki; it is now a section, 'Two pages of the same magazine, Fall 1972'. Note the Kanawana-specific angle it opens: William Commanda was teaching Algonquin canoe construction to the CCA's own canoeing instructor at Kitigan Zibi in summer 1972, a few camps acquired a Commanda canoe, and Kanawana is a Weskarini Algonquin-territory camp whose canoe programme is its oldest continuous activity. No source places Kanawana among those camps -- that is now a specific askable question rather than a general one.]

priorities.description: ASK THE YMCA OF MONTREAL FOR KANAWANA STAFF PAYROLL RECORDS FROM 1972 ONWARD. Two items in this run establish that 1972 is the year Canadian camp staff started generating federal employment paper. John Latimer's 'Unemployment Insurance Changes' (Spring 1972): from 1972 counsellors and instructors in summer camps are in insurable employment, no minimum age exemption, non-citizens not exempt, teachers and nurses no longer exempt. The Summer 1972 follow-up gives the threshold -- anyone on $30.00 a week or more including room and board. And Clifford Labbett's budget article (Fall 1972) notes that the Unemployment Insurance Commission and the provincial Workmen's Compensation Board 'maintain auditors who may examine your salary and wage records at any time,' which is a reason such records were kept and retained. After 1972 there is a payroll trail on summer camp staff that does not exist before it: a route to named Kanawana staff for years the wiki currently covers only from memory. Ask specifically for payroll ledgers, T4 summaries, UIC remittance records and Workmen's Compensation filings.

priorities.description: USE THE 1972-73 'THREAT TO CAMPING' FRAME WHEN WRITING KANAWANA'S 1970s. The movement dated its own crisis precisely. John Latimer, Fall 1972: 'Camping is having difficulties... Government legislation and red tape; increased operational and land costs; more competition; more alternatives for parents and children; less public awareness; higher standards... We are being threatened and we must do something about it!' The CCA's National Camp Directors Workshop at Geneva Park, 1-4 February 1973, was titled 'The Threat to Camping -- What does Camping have to do to survive?' Two concrete cost pressures are documented in the same issues: unemployment insurance becoming payable on camp staff from 1972 at 1.4 times the employee's rate for the employer, and Ontario sales tax on camp fees above a threshold. Any account of Kanawana's own difficulties in the 1970s should be written inside this frame rather than as a story about one camp, and the wiki should say so explicitly.

priorities.description: COMPARE ERNEST THOMPSON SETON'S PUBLISHED COUNCIL RING CEREMONY AGAINST KANAWANA'S c.1925-27 SCRIPT, LINE BY LINE. Jack Eastaugh, Assistant to the Director of the Taylor Statten Camps, states in Canadian Camping Vol. 25 No. 3 (Spring 1973): 'The Indian Council Ring Ceremony, devised by Ernest Thompson Seton in the years following the first great war and refined by Taylor Statten who taught the ceremonies to camp leaders in the 20's, needs no apology and is still viable today.' Kanawana's totem pole went up in 1927 and its 'Tribes of Kanawana in Council' script is dated c. 1925-27 -- exactly those years. Eastaugh's list of standard parts (Fire Lighting, Peace Pipe Ceremony, Indian Games, Dances, Departure of Hiawatha) matches Kanawana's scripts item for item, and his rendering of the closing chant -- 'Wakonda dhe dhu' / 'Father a needy one stands before thee; I who sing am he' -- matches Kanawana's closing line 'Wakonda, dhe-dhu, wapdhin atonhe'. The work now is textual: get Seton's published ceremony (the Woodcraft League and Birch Bark Roll material, widely digitised) and set it beside the Concordia script. Eastaugh also offered 'a complete and detailed description of the rituals, ceremonies, games and organization' on request from the Taylor Statten Camps -- ask them whether that document survives, since it is the version Kanawana's leaders would have been taught. | COMPLETED 2026-09-05. Seton's Book of Woodcraft and Indian Lore (1912) downloaded from the Internet Archive and read for the ceremony sections. THE DESCENT IS A TEXT, NOT A RESEMBLANCE. (1) The Peace Pipe Ceremony, pp. 148-149, gives the fire-lighting Kanawana's Green Triangle describes in 1940 in one line -- 'he prayed to Wakonda to light the fire' -- and the invocation 'Now know we that Wakonda, whose dwelling is above the Thunder-bird, whose messenger is the Thunder-bird, hath been pleased to smile on his children, hath sent down the sacred fire' (f_4854). (2) THE CLOSING CHANT HAS A CREDIT LINE. At p. 145 Seton prints 'THE OMAHA TRIBAL PRAYER, harmonized by Prof. J. C. Fillmore' -- 'Wa-kon-da dhe-dhu Wa-pa-dhin a-ton-he' -- credited '(By permission from Alice C. Fletcher's Indian Story and Song)' and translated 'Father a needy one stands before thee; I THAT sing am he'. Kanawana's script closes 'Wakonda, dhe-dhu, wapdhin atonhe'; Eastaugh remembered 'I WHO sing am he', one word adrift after fifty years. Line of descent documented end to end: Omaha prayer -> Fletcher (1900) -> Fillmore's harmonisation -> Seton (1912) -> Statten's camps (1920s) -> Kanawana by 1927 (f_4855). (3) BLACKSTOCK'S MAZINAW FIREPLACE CARVING IS SETON'S SENTENCE WITH THE TENSES CHANGED -- which settles that the three camps' shared Wakonda material is one text, not three borrowings (f_4856). (4) WHAT THE RITE IS MADE OF: Seton's own ceremony mixes Lakota address and pipe invocations with an Omaha song from another nation, and the 'Departure of Hiawatha' in Eastaugh's list of standard parts is neither -- it is Longfellow, 1855, absent from the Book of Woodcraft (f_4857). CHANGED: council-ring.md gains a section 'The source text, read at last' and the Mazinaw finding (18 -> 19 sources, one RALPH loop); indigenous-names-and-land.md gains the five-hands provenance and the composite point (30 -> 31 sources). STILL OPEN, and the part only a person can do: Eastaugh offered 'a complete and detailed description of the rituals, ceremonies, games and organization' on request from the Taylor Statten Camps -- ask whether that document survives, since it is the version Kanawana's leaders were actually taught. Queued as p_421.

priorities.description: TEST EASTAUGH'S CLAIM ABOUT INDIGENOUS PARTICIPATION IN YMCA CAMP PROGRAMMES. Jack Eastaugh writes in Spring 1973 that 'the Y.M.C.A. camps in Eastern and Western Canada for years have welcomed the participation of, and appreciated the contribution of local Indians in their programs,' naming people from the Golden Lake, Couchiching, Georgian Bay, Brantford and Moosonee reserves working in Ontario camps. That is a claim about Kanawana's own movement which no Kanawana source has confirmed or denied. Search the YMCA of Montreal records and Kanawana staff lists for Indigenous staff or invited participants; check whether any Kanawana source names a person from Kanesatake, Kahnawake or another Quebec community. A null result is worth recording as a null result -- the article should be able to say whether Kanawana did this, not merely that the movement claimed to.

priorities.description: WRITE THE HOAX ARGUMENT INTO wiki/traditions/myths-and-legends.md AS AN ARGUMENT, NOT A VERDICT. Within eighteen months Canadian Camping printed three positions: Bob Attfield's how-to for the camp hoax (Spring 1972), Walter Greenway naming 'a hoax' among the traditions deliberately taught to new staff at pre-camp (Spring 1972), and Mary L. Northway -- co-author of The Camp Counsellor's Book, the standard Canadian text -- writing that 'Supernatural fears from spooky stories and myths about malicious ghosts have no place in the young camper's life, nor have unnecessary fears of night raids or hazing' (Summer 1973). Hartry and Attfield both volunteered the same caution about frightening children; Northway states it as a rule. A camp running a Chopsy in the 1970s was doing something the profession was actively arguing about. That is a better documented and more interesting claim than either approval or disapproval alone, and the article should say so and cite all three. | ALREADY DONE, VERIFIED 2026-09-05. myths-and-legends.md carries all three positions and carries them AS AN ARGUMENT, which is what the priority asked for: a section headed 'The camp hoax as a documented practice', Hartry's snark hunt and Attfield's how-to and Greenway's pre-camp list, then 'And the profession was not agreed about it' introducing Northway, then the summary sentence that within a year and a half the national magazine carried a how-to, a director teaching it, and the country's leading authority saying it had no place. It also carries the restraint the priority did not ask for and should have: 'None of this is evidence about Chopsy specifically. No item in the 1949-1988 run mentions Kanawana in this connection, or the name Chopsy.' Sources 24 and 25. The priority was stale, not open; closed on reading rather than on rewriting.

priorities.description: FIND THE WRITTEN RESUME OF THE FEBRUARY 1973 GENEVA PARK NATIONAL WORKSHOP. Doug Dent records that 'all sessions were recorded to allow for a written resume for all who attended.' The workshop matters to this project because A. Ross Seaman -- Kanawana's own director -- led its session on Funding, which Morley Lee of Manitoba said 'left us the most to grapple with in terms of new information.' wiki/people/a-ross-seaman.md already cites the session; the resume would give what he actually said about how a camp was funded in 1973. Search the CCA's successor body, the Trent archives (which by 1976 held the CCA's own material), and the OCA. The same search should pick up the National Code of Ethics that Val Willis was asked to compile in April 1973.

priorities.description: FIND THE ARTICLE ON MRS. ALTA KAHN PROMISED FOR THE FALL 1973 ISSUE. Canadian Camping, Summer 1973: 'A belated but gentle tip of our hat to another gracious lady who has, for many years, been a firm supporter of the Q.C.A. -- Mrs. Alta Kahn. A richly deserved honour will be bestowed on her by Q.C.A. in May and our fall edition will feature an article about her.' A long-serving Quebec Camping Association figure with a profile promised in issue 100 of this run, which is next in the extraction pass -- so read issue 100 with this specifically in mind, and if the article is there, extract it fully and consider a stub. Quebec figures in this run have been scarce enough that a full profile of one is worth taking seriously.

priorities.description: SEARCH FOR THE OCA'S 'IT'S WISE TO SUPERVISE' (1973). Advertised at $1.25 in Canadian Camping, Summer 1973, as 'An authoritative discussion on Staff Supervision in Summer Camps,' endorsed by the Ontario Camping Association and ordered from its office. It is the fifth period document on Canadian camp staff practice this read has found, after Moon's 1968 piece, the 1969 CIT study, the OCA job-negotiation guidelines (1972) and Blackstock's model contract and staff-manual outline (1973), and it is the only one specifically about supervision -- which is the act that produces a written staff assessment. Directly relevant to p_307. Search library catalogues, the OCA's successor body and the Trent archives.

priorities.description: FIND HEDLEY G. DIMOCK'S ADDRESS 'CANADIAN CAMPING -- ITS RESISTANCE TO CHANGE,' delivered to the Canadian Camping Association meeting of 2-4 March 1967. Al Knox names and dates it in Canadian Camping (Winter/Spring 1974) and recommends it for its treatment of camper development and of 'the function and influence of the camp director.' The magazine's own April 1967 conference report describes Dimock 'urging them to change from repressive to participative methods of programming,' and a Manitoba director wrote that autumn that his camp was 'heavily impressed by Hedley Dimock at the Canadian Camping Association Conference' and introducing participatory camping. The man who spent 1960-61 studying counsellor effectiveness AT KANAWANA gave the address that put 'participative camping' into the working vocabulary of Canadian camp directors, and camps were still citing it by name seven years later. Search: the OCA Conference Digests for 1966-68 (sold at cost by the association and listed in its own publications catalogue); the CCA material at Trent; Sir George Williams / Concordia's Dimock papers; and the Centre for Human Relations and Community Studies. This is a first-order lead for hedley-dimock.md and for any account of what Kanawana's own director would have been hearing in 1967. | SEARCHED AND NULL 2026-09-05 (f_4858), and note that hedley-dimock.md already carried both contemporaneous references before this pass -- the April 1967 keynote report and the autumn 1967 Manitoba director's letter. TWO SURFACES ADDED TO THE NULL: the complete cached run of Canadian Camping, 164 issues, in which 'resistance to change' occurs in ONE issue, Knox's own 1974 article -- the magazine reported the address twice and printed it never; and the Internet Archive's 22 items under creator 'Dimock, Hedley', 1931 to 2011, none of which is the address. A CAUTION NOW IN THE ARTICLE: 'Canadian Camping -- Its Resistance to Change' is Knox's wording seven years after the fact, while the contemporaneous report calls it a keynote 'on the Individual' from 'Springboard No. 1'. They may be one address or two, and the title should not be treated as the document's own until someone sees it. WHAT IS LEFT is archival: the OCA Conference Digests for 1966-68, the CCA archive the association resolved in 1973 to deposit at the University of Waterloo, the OCA fonds at Trent (p_348), and Dimock's own papers -- he taught at Sir George Williams, so Concordia is the first place to ask (add to the p_282 letter).

priorities.description: TRACE THE QUEBEC CAMPING ASSOCIATION'S PROVINCIAL CHARTER OF 1961 AND THE PAPERS THAT GO WITH IT. The Alta Kahn tribute (Canadian Camping, Fall 1973) states: 'It was through Mrs. Kahn's efforts that the Quebec Camping Association finally secured its Provincial Charter in 1961.' An incorporation is a public record: search Quebec's Registraire des entreprises for the QCA and for l'Association des camps du Quebec, and follow the charter to the directors named on it, the registered address, and any dissolution or continuance filing. That last is the practical point -- when an incorporated association winds up or merges, its records go somewhere, and this is the most concrete handle the project has yet had on where the Quebec association's accreditation files went. Related dates from the same tribute: the association's twenty-first birthday in 1958 (founding 1937), the Provincial Board co-ordinating the English and French sections with Kahn as its second president 1963-65, and Kahn still chairing the English Section's Standards Committee in 1973. | ATTEMPTED 2026-09-05, BLOCKED, AND THE BLOCK IS ABOUT THIS ENVIRONMENT (f_4859). The Registraire des entreprises search page returns HTTP 403 with 'L'acces a nos services vous est temporairement interdit en raison d'une utilisation excessive' -- tried twice, with browser headers and French language preferences. BAnQ numerique answers 200 and renders its results in JavaScript, so the HTML carries no results. NEITHER IS EVIDENCE ABOUT THE CHARTER. WHAT WAS OBTAINED: the ACQ's own about page says 'Fondee en 1961 a l'initiative de directeurs de camps de vacances' -- crediting camp directors collectively, in the same year the Alta Kahn tribute credits her efforts for the QCA's provincial charter. Compatible statements, NOT to be merged: an incorporation and a founding are different events, and whether the 1961 charter is the ACQ's legal birth is the question. BEST UNTRIED ROUTE, and it is documentary rather than a registry lookup: THE GAZETTE OFFICIELLE DU QUEBEC FOR 1961, which publishes letters patent for non-profit corporations and would give the charter's date, the corporate name it was granted under, and the petitioners' names. BAnQ holds the run. Then: the Registraire from an ordinary Quebec browser, where the same search is free and takes a minute; and the Registre des entreprises bulk dataset on Donnees Quebec.

priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR ALTA R. KAHN. The tribute read on 23 May 1973, when the Quebec Camping Association English Section made her the first Honorary President in its history, gives a full and dated life: 1908 the first Jewish teacher to graduate from Macdonald College; 1918 a founder of Montreal Hadassah; 1920 organiser of the first Junior Hadassah chapter in Canada; 1936-45 Executive Director of the Young Women's Hebrew Association; 1946-49 Executive Secretary of the Jewish Community Camps (B'nai B'rith, Jewish Laurentian Fresh Air, and Wooden Acres), where she 'instituted many new projects, including the first Pre-Camp Training Programs for Staff'; with the QCA from 1946; chairing the 1958 joint conference; QCA Standards Committee co-chair 1959-60; English Section president 1960-62; Provincial Board president 1963-65; and still on the CCA National Standards Committee in 1973. She belongs in core people/ rather than notable-alumni: her enduring significance is Quebec camping itself, and she is the person who connects Montreal Jewish community camping in the Laurentians to the standards committee that wrote what Kanawana was measured against. Search the Canadian Jewish Congress archives, Hadassah-WIZO Canada, the Gazette and the Canadian Jewish Review for an obituary.

priorities.description: WRITE THE QUEBEC STANDARDS VISITATION INTO THE KANAWANA ARTICLES USING MADELENE ALLEN'S 1974 ACCOUNT. The Director of Camp Ouareau, a member of the QCA Standards Committee, describes the provincial standards from inside an accredited Quebec camp: 'We view this tome in different lights depending on the time of year... we view it with slight trepidation as we leaf through its pages the night before the visitor is expected.' She then gave the standards AND THE MARKING SCHEME to her five CITs at the six-week point, in pairs, a week each on different sections: they interviewed the director with pencil and notebook, shadowed senior staff, were given the records of programmes and staff lists, and 'inspected the waterfront, examined the canoes, counted the toilets, and checked the outlets of the septic tanks after a heavy rain.' That is what a Quebec standards visitation covered in 1974, and it confirms a written marking scheme as well as a standards document -- two record classes to name explicitly when asking after Kanawana's accreditation file (p_339). | DONE 2026-09-05, into cit-lit-program.md rather than the article the priority named, and the placement is the argument. Madelene Allen's account is two things at once: a description of what a Quebec standards visitation covered in 1974 -- waterfront, craft, sanitation, programme records, personnel records and the director under questioning -- and a CIT TRAINING EXERCISE, since she handed her five CITs the standards AND the marking scheme at the six-week point and had them audit the camp in pairs. The second is the part no Kanawana record has an equivalent for, so it sits in the CIT article, three sections before the 1977 statement of what a CIT was owed nationally, which it precedes and outdoes. The record-shape point the priority wanted is stated there too: a written marking scheme AND a standards document, two classes to name when asking Concordia (p_339), and if Quebec re-accredited annually then what is missing is a SERIES rather than a document. The article ends the section with the honest pair of sentences: no source says Kanawana ever did anything of the kind, and no source says it did not. cit-lit-program.md 10 -> 11 sources. ONE MECHANICAL SLIP CAUGHT BY THE HARNESS: the new footnote was inserted after the first string match for the preceding entry, which was inside the article's own Research Notes comment rather than in the Sources list -- verify_harness.py failed A1 (header says 11, 10 entries present) and the entry was moved. The lesson is the same one as the 8t footnote collision earlier today: locate by structure, not by first string match.

priorities.description: MINE THE JANUARY 1975 DIRECTORY ISSUE FOR KANAWANA -- AND FOR ITS QUEBEC NEIGHBOURS. Canadian Camping Vol. 27 No. 2 (January 1975) is a Directory Issue listing all CCA member camps in each province, 20,000 copies printed, and it is in the cache as issue 103 of this read. A targeted check has already confirmed the line 'KANAWANA (1894) (YMCA)' with St. Sauveur des Monts. This is the first direct Kanawana appearance in the 1970s stretch of the read, and a national directory entry should carry founding date, sponsor, location, ages, capacity, season, fees and director's name as the association held them in 1974-75 -- a period for which this project's Kanawana record is thin. Extract the Kanawana entry in full, field by field, and extract the whole Quebec section as a snapshot of the camps Kanawana sat among. Note also that the directory prints the camp's founding year as 1894, so the association's own national listing corroborates the date. | DONE 2026-09-05. KANAWANA'S ENTRY, field by field: 'KANAWANA (1894) (YMCA)'; director Derek V. Walsh; P.O. Box 310, St. Sauveur des Monts (514-227-2414); winter office 1441 Drummond St., Montreal (514-849-5331); activities tripping, swimming, sailing, arts & crafts, C.I.T. program; capacity 90 BOYS 8-15 AND 90 GIRLS 8-15 -- an even ninety and ninety, seven years after coeducation, in a year this project's Kanawana record is otherwise thin for (f_4866). THREE UNLABELLED COLUMNS reading 'X X C' follow the address in every Quebec entry; the header row is not recoverable from this OCR, so they are left uninterpreted rather than guessed at -- C plausibly marks co-ed or 'camp' against R for resident, but no page this read can reconstruct says so. THE WHOLE QUEBEC SECTION EXTRACTED: 64 member camps with the founding year printed beside each. Sorted, KANAWANA'S 1894 IS THE EARLIEST IN THE PROVINCE BY TWELVE YEARS -- next is Brewery Mission 1906, then Oolahwan 1917, Lewis 1918, B'nai B'rith 1921, Ouareau 1922 (f_4867). The directory prints it as a plain fact of the listing rather than a contested claim, which is worth having, though it is the association's compilation of what member camps told it and not an independent test, and it covers members only. Six of the 64 were founded after 1970 and about a quarter before 1940; francophone and anglophone camps are interleaved in one alphabetical list, fifteen years after the French section formed (f_4868). quebec-camp-landscape.md 25 -> 26 sources, with the entry, the earliest-ten table, and the long tail of camps this wiki does not otherwise follow.

priorities.description: RECORD LES VOYAGEURS DE LA VERENDRYE AS A SEPARATELY ACCREDITED CAMP IN canoe-trips.md AND THE VOYAGEUR MATERIAL. The January 1975 national directory lists it in its own right, not as a Kanawana programme: 'LES VOYAGEURS DE LA VERENDRYE (YMCA); Director Derek V. Walsh; c/o Kamp Kanawana, P.O. Box 310, St. Sauveur des Monts; Activities: Wilderness, Canoe Trips, Fishing, Campcraft; Accommodation: 15 boys 13-17 / 5 girls 13-17.' Two things follow that the wiki does not currently say. First, the Quebec Camping Association treated the trip programme as a distinct wilderness camp operating out of the Kanawana site, which means it was separately accredited and would have generated its own annual visitation report. Second, the project now has a number for its scale and its gender composition in 1975: twenty places, fifteen boys' and five girls', ages 13 to 17 -- the girls' places existed but were a quarter of the boys'. Kanawana's own entry in the same directory gives 90 boys and 90 girls aged 8-15 at exactly equal capacity, so the trip programme's imbalance is not explained by the main camp's.

priorities.description: FIND THE MINUTES OF THE CCA ANNUAL MEETING OF OCTOBER 1974, HELD IN MONTREAL. Stated twice in the April 1975 issue, in the tributes to F. M. Van Wagner and Charles Plewman, both made Honorary Members there. A national camping association annual meeting in Kanawana's own city, in a year for which this project's Quebec record is thin, whose minutes would name the Quebec camps and people present -- and Kanawana's director was on the QCA English Section executive at the time. The same search should pick up the QCA Director and Senior Staff Seminar held in Montreal 14-16 March 1975 with Dr. Don Ehat as keynote, which Wilfred A. Jackson announces in the same issue.

priorities.description: CHASE THE 1975 CONFERENCE TAPES ON STAFF SUPERVISION AND EVALUATION. The CCA's publications catalogue (April 1975) sells seventeen cassette tapes of the January 1975 Geneva Park national conference at $4.00 each, ten of them Canadian sessions: 'Recruiting, Hiring, Interviewing' (Bruce Harris), 'Evaluating Your Camp' (Barry Lowes), 'Staff Training' (John Boutin), 'Staff Supervision' (Brian Law), 'Develop Staff From Within Your Camp' (Al Knox), plus budget, recruiting and PR, camp philosophy and committees. A recorded, purchasable 1975 seminar on camp staff supervision and evaluation is directly relevant to p_307, and cassettes sold in quantity to member camps sometimes survive where paper does not. Ask the CCA's successor body and the Trent holdings. The same catalogue lists two new Canadian titles to find: the Camp Counsellor's Handbook by Blackstock and Latimer (1975, 128 pp.) and Tolbitt's Counsellor's Guide to Camp Singing (44 pp.), the nearest thing yet found to the national camp songbook p_311 is chasing.

priorities.description: UPDATE derek-walsh.md WITH HIS QUEBEC ASSOCIATION CHRONOLOGY. Two independent sightings in this run fix it: the January 1975 Directory Issue lists him as Director of both Kanawana and Les Voyageurs de la Verendrye, and as chairman of the QCA English Section's Publicity and Public Relations committee; by October 1976 the stub already has him as President of the Section. So the presidency followed a committee chairmanship in the same portfolio he would later hold nationally. The directory also gives his name with the middle initial -- Derek V. Walsh -- and corroborates the stub's 1974-to-February-1979 directorship from an independent source. Note in the same article that A. R. Seaman, Kanawana's director of 1959-67, was an Honorary Member of the same Section in January 1975: two Kanawana directors on the provincial association's English Section at once.

priorities.description: RECORD THE 1976 YMCA LIFESAVING CHANGEOVER IN THE WATERFRONT MATERIAL. Doug Dent, Canadian Camping, January 1976: 'First of all, the YMCA lifesaving program was revamped, and in its place the RLSS program (Bronze Medallion and upwards) has been adopted.' So by 1976 the YMCA had dropped its own lifesaving programme for the Royal Life Saving Society's. The same article prints a three-column equivalence chart -- YMCA Pre-Beginner, Beginner and Star I-VI against Red Cross Pre-Beginner, Beginner, Junior, Intermediate and Senior, and RLSS Survival and Life Saving I, II and III (the RLSS having just replaced its Elementary and Intermediate levels). This matters for reading any Kanawana swimming record: the YMCA 'Star' levels are the system a Kanawana swimmer of the period would have been graded on, and an award named in a camper's memory or a staff list can now be placed against a national scale and dated either side of the 1976 changeover.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 106-109, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: WRITE THE THREE STRUCTURAL BREAKS IN THE CANADIAN CAMPING RUN INTO meta/sources-index.md (see p_359). The run has three dated interruptions in three years, and each explains an apparent hole: publication was SUSPENDED in February 1974 on financial grounds by the CCA Board and resumed only in November 1974 (Vol. 26 No. 2 is a combined Winter/Spring 1974 number, then nothing until Vol. 27 No. 1); the November 1975 number is a FOUR-PAGE NEWSLETTER because the Canadian postal strike left the editor short of advertisements and of the French-language content; and the June 1976 issue announces itself as the LAST -- 'The decision was made by the CCA Board at the recent meetings in Quebec City and was one based wholely on financial considerations' -- after which the title continues from October 1976 as a typewritten eight-page newsletter, five or six numbers a year instead of quarterly. So the format and depth change sharply at issue 109 of this read, and nothing is missing from the project's holdings at any of the three points. The section should say all of this before it says anything about content.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 106-109, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: CHECK QUEBEC'S STATUTORY RECORD FOR CAMP WATERFRONT AND SAFETY REGULATION FROM 1976 -- AND FOR A GOVERNMENT INSPECTION FILE ON KANAWANA. Canadian Camping's Quebec column, December 1976: 'A somewhat scary proposal is now being made by the Department of Labour...Waterfronts in camps may not be deeper than six feet!!!' The exclamation marks are the association's. In the same months the High Commission of Leisure and Sports was paying for a full-time provincial camp training post and, by February 1977, giving the association $300,000 for its spring training programme -- so the Quebec government was funding the accrediting body and drafting rules of its own at the same time. Two questions follow. Was the six-foot rule ever enacted, in any form? A depth limit is not something a camp on a natural lake can comply with by adjusting anything, so if it passed it would have forced visible changes at every Laurentian camp. And if a ministry was regulating camp waterfronts from 1976-77, there may be a GOVERNMENTAL inspection file on Kanawana distinct from the association's annual accreditation reports (p_314). Search: Quebec's Gazette officielle and statutory instruments for 1976-80; the Haut-Commissariat a la Jeunesse, aux Loisirs et aux Sports fonds and the ministere du Travail fonds at BAnQ.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 110-113, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR CHARLES F. PLEWMAN. The read has justified it four times over and the biography is now fully dated: born about 1889-90 (he was 87 in February 1977); first at camp as a camper in 1903; ran his first short-term camp in 1909; Director of Camp On-Da-Da-Waks 1913-1916, then three years at Camp Stephens, then Inter-Church camps; eight years YMCA Boys' Work Secretary at Ottawa and Winnipeg and eleven years Secretary for the Ontario Boys' Work Board -- the same office Roy Locke and Nelson McEwen held at Montreal; founded Kilcoo Camp in 1932 and owned it to 1955; OCA president from 1945; Secretary of the Toronto branch of the Canadian Red Cross in the Second World War, where he instituted the Toronto Mobile Blood Donor Service; Honorary Fellow of the Society of Camp Directors at its 1969 inaugural dinner; Honorary Member of the CCA at the Montreal annual meeting of October 1974. He matters to this project for three separate reasons: he founded the magazine that is this project's largest single source and wrote its founding history; he is a first-hand witness on the CCA's own founding (c_035), on both 1936 and 1946; and he published an eyewitness account of Tom Thomson's burial fifty-five years after the event. Place in core people/ only if the wider-lens test is met -- otherwise connections/institutional-lineage/.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 110-113, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR FRANCES M. KELLY. She appears across twenty-five years of this run in the same office: secretary at the Quebec Camping Association English Section in the early 1950s, Executive Secretary through the 1960s and 1970s at 2233 Belgrave Avenue, chairman of its Staff Placement Bureau in 1975, author of the F. M. Van Wagner tribute in 1975 that gave this project the QCA's founding date and the 1955 Manual of Standards, and singled out at the fortieth anniversary conference in March 1977 for "special recognition" as "the backbone of the English section of Q.C.A." She is the person who would have handled Kanawana's membership, its accreditation correspondence and its staff placement listings for a quarter-century, which makes her the most likely single custodian of the records p_314 is looking for -- and a person to trace for surviving papers or family. Search Montreal directories, the Gazette, and the association's successor body.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 110-113, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: SPAWN A STUB FOR EILEEN MAYOTTE -- and note the Quebec connection. Her CCA executive profile of February 1978: 'During her illustrious career in camping, Eileen has had responsibility for camps and campers in four provinces -- Ontario, Quebec, Saskatchewan, and B.C. Her camping endeavors have lead her into church camping, YWCA and camps for underprivileged children. In the distant past she was the Secretary of the Quebec Camping Association. She was one of the founders of the Saskatchewan Camping Association, and for many years was its President.' She appears through this run as Saskatchewan president from 1970, as the author of the clearest statement of camper agency in it (Responsibility, 1976, on Ginott: 'the selecting belongs to the administration -- the choosing should be the right of the camper'), as CCA Secretary from April 1977 and Vice-President from November 1977. The Quebec secretaryship is undated and is the thing to pin down: she held the office A. Ross Seaman held from about 1949, at some earlier point, which would put her in Kanawana's own provincial association. Search Quebec Camping Association records, YWCA Montreal, and Saskatchewan press.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 114-117, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: GET A QUEBEC DELEGATE LIST FOR THE GENEVA PARK NATIONAL CONFERENCES. Delegates to the CCA's national conferences were SELECTED BY EACH PROVINCIAL ASSOCIATION rather than by application -- the October 1977 announcement of the third conference (19-22 January 1978, theme 'Keys to Success', $75 per delegate with return air fare covered from outside Ontario by Recreation Canada) says so explicitly. So a Quebec delegate list for January 1978 is a short, checkable document naming who the association sent, and Kanawana's own director was that association's English-section president at the time. The same applies to the January 1975 and February 1973 conferences. Ask the Quebec association's successor body and Trent; the 1973 conference also produced a written resume of every session (p_372) and seventeen cassette tapes.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 114-117, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: ASK CONCORDIA FOR KANAWANA'S PER-BUILDING MAINTENANCE RECORDS BY NAME. Wilfred A. Jackson, Director of Camps and Conference Centre for Catholic Community Services in Montreal and chairman of the QCA English Section's fortieth anniversary conference, set out in Canadian Camping (April 1978) exactly what a Montreal camp administrator of the period was told to keep: a MASTERPLAN showing all buildings present and future; a loose-leaf MAINTENANCE MANUAL with check lists, directions and 'a schedule arranged by seasons, including specific details on opening and closing procedures'; and 'A record of each building should be kept showing floor plans, type of construction, history, inventory, and required repairs', with plans of the water, electrical and sewage systems and manufacturers' instructions on file. He adds a large master map, a portfolio of buildings with photographs and floor plans, a LOG OF IMPROVEMENTS, a list of local suppliers kept in the maintenance building, and tagged keys with spares held by the maintenance head. If Kanawana kept any of this, site/the-kanawana-site.md and meta/plaque-audit.md have an unexploited source class -- a per-building file with floor plans and repair history, which is precisely what a plaque audit needs. Ask by these names; a request for 'building records' will not find them.
priorities.source: word-for-word read of Canadian Camping, issues 118-122, converted to KB facts

priorities.description: SEARCH THE QUEBEC HEALTH DEPARTMENT'S RECORD FOR LAKE KANAWANA WATER SAMPLES. Eanswythe Flynn's checklist tells directors, in May and again in June of every year covered by this run, to 'Send water samples (both drinking and swimming) regularly to Provincial Health Department.' For an accredited camp this was not optional -- water tested before camp and re-tested weekly is item after item in the printed standards. A routine of that kind, kept up over decades, generates a dated series in the provincial health record: sample dates, results, and the name and address of the submitting camp. That would independently date Kanawana's operating seasons, and a failed sample would date a problem. Search: the ministere de la Sante fonds and its predecessors at BAnQ, the regional health unit for the Laurentians, and any municipal record for Saint-Sauveur. Pair this with p_388, which asks the same question of the labour ministry's camp waterfront rule.
